Mr. Speaker, I would ask the indulgence of the House for a few minutes while I bring to its attention a .matter of considerable importance, not only to the county which I represent, but to the Dominion of Canada in general. We have at present in this country a state of affairs in which the revenues are decreasing and the expenditures are not being correspondingly reduced. I think this is a good time for the government to cut out all expenditures that are practically useless. One of these is the expenditure on what is known as the Newmarket canal in the county of York. This so-called canal extends from Cook's bay to Newmarket, and is in two sections. The portion from Cook's bay to Holland Landing, is section No. 1, and the portion from Holland Landing to Newmarket is section No. 2. We understand, from the statement of the Hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, that there has been no expenditure on section No. 1, which in my opinion is the only part that could be made of any particular use at all. Section No. 2 is the expensive part, and on this so far there has been expended nearly $200,000. The estimated cost of the canal is nearly $1,000,000, although as yet no accurate estimate of its cost has been made. In my opinion, the expenditure on this canal is an absolute waste of public money. I have spoken to a good many people in the county of York in regard to this canal, and every person to whom I have spoken is of the same opinion, that it is an utterly useless work. The hon. gentleman who represents that constituency in parliament (Hon. A. B. Ayles-worth) disclaims any responsibility or credit for this canal, saying that it was instituted before he entered parliament. I understand that it was started in 1904, although no work of any extent was done on it until the year 1908, as expended previous to March 31, 1908, $31,444.26; expended since March 31, 1908, the following figures

The first estimate of the cost of this canal made in April, 1905, was $291,249; the second estimate, made on June 19, 1908, was $967,814.50; and these estimates did not include reservoirs south of Newmarket for the conservation of the water to be used in the canal, which according to the reports of the engineers are necessary. We have no accurate estimate of the cost of these reservoirs. The hon. gentleman who represents North York said that there was only one opinion in that constituency in regard to this canal. In that I entirely agree with him: There is only one opinion, so far as I have heard, and that is that the canal is absolutely useless. Even if it were feasible, there is no business for it to warrant such a great expenditure by the government. There has been spent on the work already nearly $200,000, and the hon. gentleman who represents the constituency asks if it would be wise to throw away $200,000. I think it would be better to throw away $200,000 now than to throw away $2,000,000 in the future. My reason for bringing this matter before the House is entirely non-political. The constituency of Centre York, which never before, since 1867, elected a Conservative to parliament, has sent me here, by the votes of independent men, to give my best ability to looking after the expenditure of public money. There may be other parts of the Dominion where public money is being expendeid as lavishly and wastefully as it is in this particular work, but I do not know so much about them. I do know, however, about this work, and I ask the House to take into its_ serious consideration the expenditure of this large sum of money on a canal which, not only in my opinion, but in the opinion of every man who knows anything about it, is absolutely useless. For these reasons. I desire to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word * that ' in the proposed resolution be omitted and the following substituted therefor:
The original estimate of the cost of the proposed canal between Newmarket and Lake Simcoe, in the riding of North York, was less than $300,000; but that estimate has now been increased to nearly $1,000,000, which latter sum, according to the engineer's report, does not include the proposed expenditure for conservation of water south of Newmarket;
That the total cost of the said canal when completed is as yet unestimated and can only be conjectured;
That the said canal when so completed will be practically useless; that the expenditure thereon is wholly improvident and unwarranted, and constitutes a wanton misuse and waste of public money.

However, it is not a matter that need occupy a great deal of time. It might not be out of place for me to say a word or two on the canals of the world generally, to show the important part they play in the transportation problem.

We have in Canada altogether completed 109J miles and something over 200 miles partly completed. There are 102 locks. These do not include the lift-locks on the Trent. In these canals we have 20 dams.
There will be more in this.

I mean dams for the retention of water. This question of transportation by water is of course a very large one, and one of great significance. My hon. friend talks of the expenditure on the Newmarket canal. He says it will cost a lot of money and that it will be useless. To his first proposition I agree, but from the second I dissent. The canal, if we are to take the word of men who ought to know as engineers, is a perfectly feasible proposition, and will, when completed, furnish navigation equal to the Erie, which for years has carried the grain trade of the west from Buffalo to New York
Is the grain trade of the west going through this?

My hon. friend cannot tell what may happen, but to-day it is not, as the canal is not yet constructed. Regarding the water supply, some one has made merry over the possibility of the Minister of Justice and myself having to use a pump handle to get water into that canal. I think I have seen a cartoon to that effect. Well, it may be surprising to know that some of the canals in other countries are aided in their water supply by a pumping system from artesian wells. I want to call attention to a very important work on canals by Mr. Harcourt which deals with the question of their water supply. He proves that the majority of canals would be dry and useless were it not that their water supply is conserved by dams or other means. I ask the patience of the House while I read from this work *on page 365:-

An adquate supply of water must be provided for a oanal, to make good losses from leakage, evaporation, and expenditure of water in locking. Frequently this supply can be furnished by adjacent streams, or by the main river in the case of a lateral canal, or sometimes by a lake, springs, artesian wells or pumping; but when a constant supply is not procurable from these sources, which is especially liable to be the case at the summit level of a canal, an artificial reservoir must be formed, at a sufficient elevation, by plaoing a dam across the valley of a water course, which being filled in the winter, is able to furnish the neoessary quantity of water to the canal throughout the dry season.
This is the principle which is being applied to the canal in question:-
The largest reservoirs, dams for impounding water in artificial reservoirs in the valleys of rivers, have been constructed for the water supply of towns and for irrigation, to which branches of engineering the formation of reservoirs mainly belongs. Nevertheless, many canals are partially supplied, particularly in their upper reaohes, by numerous reservoirs which have been mestly formed by means of earthen reservoir dams placed across the valleys of small rivers at suitable points. Thus the Grand Junction canal is fed by eight reservoirs along the Tring, summit level, and by two reservoirs at the Braunston summit level, having a total oapacity of 7k million cubic yards, and the Leeds and Liverpool canal is supplied by six reservoirs with a capacity of 5J million cubio yards, and the Rochdale oanal navigation by seven reservoirs with a capacity of 9i million cubic yards. The Crinan canal draws its supply from nine reservoirs, having a capacity of million cubic yards; whilst the Caladonian canal is fed by the lakes through whioh it passes, and the Ellesmere canal by Bala lake as well as by two reservoirs.
Just another quotation from this work:-
The principal reservoirs, however, in Russia have been formed by dams across the upper portions of rivers, closed on the melting of the snow to provide water for navigation in

the river below during the summer. These dams, which constitute in reality draw-door weirs, are generally made entirely of wood, though sometimes masonry piers have been introduced, and the head of water retained does not exoeed 17i feet.
It may be asked why I quote from this work. Simply to point out to hon. gentlemen, who seem not to take the time to think it out along this line, that very few canals would be practicable were it not for a system of reservoirs as is proposed in the case of the Newmarket canal. The canal system, except in the case of canals along rivers such as the St. Lawrence, is based on the fact that there is water which can be conserved and forced into use either by power or by the use of dams. It would be impossible to have navigation to-day on the Trent canal, just as it would be in the Newmarket portion of that canal, if dams were not used. Every one who has gone through the Trent Valley canal must be aware of that. I can remember when men on both sides made jests, making light of the Trent Valley canal in any of its reaches, just as my hon. friend makes light of the Newmarket branch. When our Conservative friends were in office, the Liberal opposition pointed out that the Trent Valley canal was a mere ditch used more for mere political purposes than for practical reasons. And our friends opposite when in opposition, made the same references to that canal when it was out of their control. But owing to the scientific placing of dams and reservoirs there is going to be from Georgian bay to Lake Ontario a system of navigation which will be better than the Erie canal ever has been, which has carried the grain trade from the west to the east.
I think I speak with good authority when I say that the Newmarket section of the Trent canal will be as navigable in every part as the Erie canal is at the present time. Take the history of the work. As my hon. friend has pointed out, the estimate made was much smaller than the cost will be. But I think it is only fair to point out to him that the cost of materials and labour at the present time is at least from thirty to fifty per cent higher than it was three or four years ago, or perhaps, two years ago. In the construction of new works, where contracts are asked for, the Railway Department find that prices have risen, and when we make purchases we find that the prices are much higher than they were two or three years ago. Leaving aside that argument, and taking the mere fact that the cost will be more than the estimate, I want to say that the canal will be as practicable as any other portion of the Trent canal.
My hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) has read the reports, but I have before me only a brief synopsis. On July 17, 1905, Mr. Walsh
reports on the work and points out that he had investigated the question of the sufficiency of water supply for the operation of the canal, and that he had weir measurements taken of the main stream and its chief tributaries about Newmarket. He states that the measurements were made during the preceding winter-the winter of 1904-5-after a dry season of two months' duration, during which numerous wells and other sources of water supply had gone dry that, he was informed, seldom failed.
As the hon. minister is dealing with that point, will he tell us what the estimated average number of cubic feet per minute will be?
I shall come to that in a little while. If I leave this part of the matter, I may not get back to it again.
That estimate of Walsh's is altogether wrong.

I will come to the estimates that have been made. The result of Mr. Walsh's test showed an average flow of 30,420 cubic feet of water per hour. He further said that it was safe to assume that at no season of the year would the amount fall below this. He points out that to fill one of the locks would require about 28,000 cubic feet of water, and consequently a supply for the lock could be furnished in fifty-five minutes without damming or impounding water, but that he proposed to build dams at suitable places for storing freshet water and to have side ponds approximately close to the locks. It is the usual practice as I have stated, to supply water for the canals, except in the cases I have mentioned. Mr. Walsh goes on to give a computation of the drainage area tributary to Newmarket, and after making due allowance for loss through evaporation, &c., concludes that the available rainfall, which he takes at only one-sixth of the whole rainfall, would be 174,240,000 cubic feet. He concludes his report as follows:
In the meantime, I consider that sufficient data is afforded to establish beyond question the fact that the proposed canalization of the section of the Holland river between Newmarket and Holland landing, and the proposed improvements of the river between the latter place and Cook's bay is in every respect feasible.
That was the report of the engineer at that time, a report any department would be justified in proceeding upon, and that the House felt itself justified in proceeding upon. In the final report of Mr. Walsh, dated September 29, 1906, Mr. Walsh summarizes the question of water supply and states that the east branch of the Holland river above Newmarket has a drainage area of approximately sixty-one square miles, with an average annual rainfall from 1896 to 1905 of 30-67 inches. The annual precipitation of the whole watershed is, therefore,

3,921,259,584 cubic feet, and allowing for loss through evaporation, absorption by plants, &c., and, for this purpose deducting sixty per cent, he finds that the available water -which runs off to Lake Simcoe-for storage purposes is 1,568,503,834 cubic feet. The stream between Newmarket and Holland Landing has a drainage area of about fourteen square miles; it is not, however, thought necessary to consider this additional source of supply. The minimum flow of water in the stream above Newmarket was fcund to be 507 cubic feet per minute. This was ascertained by careful weir measurements taken at the very lowest stage of water, at the dryest season of the year and after a prolonged drought of two months' duration.
Now, would the hon. minister give the report of Mr. Grant on the same point, which he read here in answer to a question from myself some weeks ago?

I am going to give them all before I get through. I have a synopsis here of the three reports. To ascertain the feasibility and cost of supplementing the water supply to which I have referred, extensive surveys were made at several suitable places on the watershed for establishing storage reservoirs. The tabulated report on this point has been laid on the table. Mr. Walsh selected Lake Wilcocks, on the height of land-known as 'the Oak Ridge'-between lakes Simcoe and Ontario, the source of the Humber river, as being the best additional source of supply should it be found necessary to resort to the same, but, in his opinion, not required. After discussing a number of other points as sources of supply, he concludes, on page 9 of his report, that it would be possible to lock through a total of 4,707 vessels, or about twenty per day during seven months of each year, providing all the sources named by him were used. He gives his estimate, which, as my hon. friend has pointed out, is too low, amounting to $354,536. The storage capacity provided for in his proposed plans aggregates 88,667,925 cubic feet.
Now, let me go a little more into the history of the work as it has proceeded, givr ing also a digest of Mr. Grant's findings. Let us take section 2, Holland river divir sion. On February 12, 1908, Mr. Grant, who is one of the most efficient engineers in the whole department, after giving the results of the analysis, points out that the rainfall for 1907, which was a very dry year, was somewhat less than 30 inches, still showing that there was ample rainfall to operate the canal, if properly conserved. Mr. Grant himself has gone over the figures very carefully, and, in his report of 1907, although he finds that the rainfall was less than thirty inches, and less, than Mr. Walsh found it, there is still Mr. GRAHAM.
ample water to operate the canal. A good deal has been said about the necessity for conserving the water. I have discussed that point. As a matter of fact, we have to conserve the water on the Rideau canal, the Chambly, the Carillon and others-probably nine-tenths of the canals are run on this principle. The Erie canal could not exist but for the conservation of water by reservoirs and dams. Whatever differences of opinion may exist as to the traffic that may arise incident to this branch of the canal, or whatever differences of opinion may exist as to this work from a commercial standpoint, no doubt exists in my mind, and I think no doubt can exist in the mind of any person who bases his opinion on the statement of practical engineers, that there will be more than sufficient water to carry all the traffic that can be carried on the Trent Valley canal. I am not going to dilate on the trade of the county of York. Several gentlemen interested in trade not only in Newmarket, but in the city of Toronto, have spoken to me of the benefit to come to the city of Toronto if the canal were completed from the Georgian bay even to this Newmarket canal. I am not going to discuss that, because it is a question I have not gone into; I refer to it because one or two who are level headed business men have told me that I was free to say that in their opinion it would be a great benefit to the trade of Toronto to get water navigation direct north after a few miles of railway haul to join the Trent Valley system to Newmarket. The county of York is perhaps one of the most important counties in the Dominion of Canada. Not to impress my hon. friend with the fact of its greatness or with its traffic, I took some pains to gather statistics to find out the business done in the county of York. I find that the value of lands and buildings in that county is $30,000,000; field crops, $4,000,000; fruits and vegetables, $465,212. These figures are taken from the last census, the products of the county have largely increased since then. Value of animals killed and sold, $1,343,369 in thei year the census was taken. I find that the total manufactures in the county of York amounted to something over $14,000,000. That does not include the city of Toronto, but the region of the county outside the city of Toronto. I merely call attention to these figures, to point out the importance of that county. I wish further to say that if the building of this canal to Newmarket, or to any other point in the centre of that thriving and prosperous county where there are manufacturers as well as agricultural industries would tend to cheapen freight rates in any way, and bring to the people a lesser rate of freight for their goods coming in or their products going out, I think it would be sufficient benefit to warrant this

great outlay, because all the many millions we are spending throughout Canada on transportation has that one object in view.
The country is committed to building the Newmarket canal. It has cost a great deal more money than was estimated. In that particular regard it is not alone because nearly all the great works that are undertaken, either by private individuals or by public corporations, have cost a great deal more than their first estimate. If any of my hon. friends have undertaken to build even a modest house, they must have found that out. But in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to the cost -and I say this on account of the resolution of my hon. friend who states that it is only a conjecture-I may state that the cost as estimated by Mr. Grant is, as my hon. friend has pointed out, nearly a million dollars. Mr. Butler has estimated that the reservoir will cost $80,000; I think that will fully cover it. The canal itself will cost in the vicinity of a million dollars; it will be a benefit, and will be promoted as a means of transportation for any boats that can go through any other part of the Trent Valley canal system. These being the circumstances of the case, I think my hon. friend, while I disagree with him as to the cost, is altogether wrong in asking the House to vote for the resolution which says this canal will be practically of no use whatever. I submit to the House that it will be of use, that it will be of as much use as any other branch of the Trent! canal; and in conclusion I must ask the House to allow us to proceed to its completion and make it, as I believe it will be, an important branch of the transportation system.	f
Before the minister concludes, will he give us an idea of the probable tonnage that will go over it?
As I told the House the other evening, I have made no estimate of the tonnage.

As this Newmarket canal is being constructed in a constituency that adjoins the one I have the honour to represent, I desire to trespass a few minutes on the attention of the House to speak in support of this resolution. It is not my intention to follow the minister so far afield as to ascertain and calculate the canal mileage of the world. The minister in his statement to the House, agrees that the canal is going to be a very costly undertaking; he also says it is going to be feasible. But that is a very flexible word; what is feasible may not be expedient or desirable in the interest of the country. The main question, in my opinion, is whether the canal is going to serve any useful public purpose. If it is not, then it is not in the interest of this country to incur such a large expense, particularly when the times are so stringent that it is necessary to curtail the expenditure of the country. When the minister was reading about canals which could only be made navigable by adopting an artesian well or a pumping system, I drew a picture in my mind's eye of a thousand electors in North York working pumps at election time at $2 a day to fill this canal. The Minister of Railways and Canals also stated that the original estimate was laregly exceeded, that the original estimate was something around $300,000, but that subsequent estimates which largely increased this amount were due to the increased cost of materials. I think he placed the increased cost of materials at from 40 to 50 per cent. But he failed to inform us that the original estimate had been increased some 300 per cent. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is an absurd comparison, to compare a canal that is connecting Cook's bay at Lake Simcoe with a dead end at Newmarket, with a great canal such as the Welland or Erie canals. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals also took pains to gather statistics in regard to the great industrial prosperity of the county of York. It is a wonder that the hon. gentleman and his colleagues, before they initiated this project which is going to cost between a million and two million dollars, did not collect some statistics to show what the possible tonnage might be on this canal. You would think, Mr. Speaker, that the first consideration of the hon. gentlemen opposite, before embarking upon an expenditure of this kind, would have been to calculate the possible tonnage that would utilize this waterway.
But, Sir, this unique canal has certainly a very interesting history. It was first mooted prior to the general elections of 1904. It was initiated on the petition of nine electors, only nine electors of North York. They petitioned merely for the deepening and straightning of the Holland and Black rivers. So that it started as a very small and insignificant undertaking; but like the proverbial snowball it gathers in proportion and momentum as it goes along. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that no person within a radius of thirty or forty miles considers it other than as a political undertaking, certainly not a commercial undertaking. North York, as we know, is represented by the hon. the Minister of Justice; prior to his advent to this House it was represented by Sir Wm. Mulock, and it always had a normal Reform majority of 700 or 800. But when Mr. Lennox, a young Conservative, captured the constituency for the local legislature, consternation seized the Liberal workers. Something had to be undertaken in order to hold the seat for the Dominion House. Consequently a council

of war was held to consider ways and means of spending the public money in the interest of the party. No person pretended to suggest that it would serve any useful public purpose. But the main object and purpose was to devise some means whereby the public moneys might be spent in North York in such a way as to save the constituency to the federal House. For all (the good the canal is, they might have suggested building a railway to the moon, because no person considers seriously that it is of any commercial utility whatever. But they proposed the building of this canal, no doubt because it will cost more money, and the present generation will certainly not live to see its com; pletion. No doubt, in the view of those who initiated this foolish project, it will be a never-failing source of income to generations of young Liberals yet unborn.
What are the cold facts in connection with this canal? The distance from Lake Simcoe to Newmarket is 10J miles. The difference in elevation between the town of Newmarket and the water in Lake Sim-coe is 45 feet. The whole project is based on the report of an engineer dated March 17, 1905, in which he says:
This canal would, in my opinion, prove of great advantage to the towns of Holland Landing and Newmarket and the country tributary to those, and more especially to the latter town, where there are several thriving industries which should be a valuable feeder to the main Trent canal.
The engineer talks about the town of Holland Landing. I endeavoured to ascertain where the town of Holland Landing is situated. I looked up the list of mayors, boards of trade and directories, but I could not find any trace of the town of Holland Landing. I looked up the post offices and ascertained that Holland Landing consisted of 79 houses and 446 persons. The town of Newmarket has a population of 2,125, and a postal revenue in 1908 of $5,297. The real estate assessment of Newmarket is $714,865, and the real estate assessment of Holland Landing is $66,249, for a total real estate assessment of $781,114. These are the important commercial metropolises that this great canal is to serve. The expenditure on the project will exceed the assessed values of the two towns mentioned by the engineer. When the engineer drafted that report he knew he was deliberately misleading the authorities, and the authorities should have made further inquiries before embarking on such an undertaking. The estimates of expenditures on public works always show great elasticity when prepared by government engineers. The estimated cost of this project as given in an estimate dated March 17, 1905, was $291,249.86. On July IT, 1905, a few months afterwards, the expenditure was estimated at over $300,000. On Febru-Mr. S. bHARPE.
ary 20, 1909, the estimated expenditure was $967,814.50. In addition to that last estimated expenditure the engineer puts a rider:
The above estimate does not include any sum for conservation of water south of Newmarket, and I do not know what this item will cost as no plans or estimates have yet been prepared for storage reservoirs.
The steady increase in the estimated cost of this work shows the utter incapacity of the engineers and indicates that no reliance should be placed on their reports. Then there is no estimate for land damages, which will amount to thousands and thousands of dollars. I would suggest that the First Minister should take a trip into North York and see what an undertaking this is, how much damage is being done to the land and how many thousands we are paying for lands in addition to the real construction of the canal. There are four different road crossings to be provided for, and they will be overcome by overhead crossings with concrete abutments and steel superstructures. Then there are to be 4 or 5 locks between Holland Landing and Newmarket, and there must be dams and storage reservoirs to impound sufficient water to make the canal navigable. Houses for lock tenders must be constructed at considerable expense and the land damages will be very heavy. The annual upkeep must also be high. Interest charges at 5 per cent on the total cost will amount to about $100,000 per annum. In addition to that there are wages of lock-tenders and expenses of operation coming to at least $5,000, so that the annual upkeep or expense to the country for the canal after its completion must not be less than $105,000.
T|fe question naturally suggests itself: what public utility is this canal going to serve? There are in my opinion two insuperable barriers to its successful operation :	In the first place there is no water
and in the second place, if there were water, there is no traffic for which the canal could be used. I am not surprised that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), when the estimates for this work were being put through, refused to defend this in a vigorous and whole-hearted manner. He called upon the Minister of Justice to defend this peculiar expenditure which is to be made in his constituency. The Minister of Justice shifts the responsibility on his predecessor, the late Postmaster General; each endeavours to shift the responsibility on some one else. The Minister of Justice is so legal and judicial in his temperament that he does not like to be bothered with embarrassing questions of fact. We saw that yesterday in connection with the Canada Life Bill. When there was a simple question of fact to decide he shifted the responsibility to the Banking and Commerce Committee and

said he would accept their dictum. The other day when defending this estimate, he said: I rely upon the engineers; they ascertain as a question of fact whether it is feasible or not and I accept their dictum. The rest of us are confronted from day to day by embarrassing questions of fact and we have to find a solution for these questions of fact; I do not see why the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) does not apply a little common sense to these matters and decide these questions of fact for himself. I desire to say with all seriousness that this canal is an object of great curiosity in North York. There is no use side-stepping these questions, the construction of this canal is a political and not a commercial undertaking, it is useless to consider this question without calling a spade a spade. The residents of North York themselves say that it is ridiculous; the newspapers are a unit in denouncing this gross, wanton and useless extravagance. The people for miles around drive to see it as a curiosity. As the hon. member for York (Mr. Wallace) so well said, when the government are curtailing expenditures in other departments, why do they go on with the extravagant expenditure in connection with this work? Take the estimates for agriculture. You will find that the miserable sum of $931,000 has been appropriated for that industry, the staple industry of this country. The appropriation for this year was cut from $130,000 to $98,000 for experimental farms, a reduction of $30,000 and yet hundreds of thousands of dollars are being squandered on the North York canal. So with the votes for the development of the fruit industry, the encouragement of the growing of pure seed, the encouragement of the raising of live stock, and experimental farms, health of animals, There is a total reduction in the votes for agriculture this year of $585,500, and yet we see hundreds of thousands sunk on this waterless ditch. There are only $98,000 for experimental farms and there are $1,000,000 for the North York canal. There is a reduction of $585,500 in the estimates for the most important and staple industry in this country and $1,000,000 for the canal which will be of no use unless the government can devise a means of making water run up hill, in defiance of the laws of gravitation. One million dollars would accomplish a great deal in the encouragement of the agricultural industry. It would establish 40 experimental farms at $25,000 each or it would establish and equip 20 hospitals for the treatment of preventive diseases at $50,000 each. I say that it would be in the interest of the country and to the credit of the government if they would take a sensible and proper stand upon this question and stop all operations on that so called canal. Let them put up for sale the
land they have expropriated and let them discontinue this absolutely useless scheme. Such a stupendous undertaking as this should not have been lightly entered upon by the government, and the conclusions that should have moved them to initiate it were twofold, namely: was the scheme practical and if practical was it expedient? Certainly neither of these could have influenced the government or otherwise this work never would have been commenced. No words are too strong to criticise this bizarre and fantastical undertaking because it is nothing else. It is an insult to the intelligence of the electors of Canada to have hundreds of thousands of dollars squandered on this ridiculous project. I agree with the concluding paragraph of the motion which says:-
That the said canal when so completed will be practically useless; that the expenditure thereon is wholly improvident and unwarranted and constitutes a wanton misuse and waste of public money.

Some two or three years ago when this project was first proposed to the House it was described as the Holland river and Newmarket canal, and we all knew what we were voting for, but for some reason or other later on the government hid it in a general vote for the Trent Valley canal, a proceeding which was unfair to the members of the House, because I know there are many hon. gentlemen here who would have entered a strong protest against it last year were they not deceived by the new title it got in the estimates. When the scheme was first proposed I protested and I expressed the opinion that the House was wasting time in discussing the question of the water supply, because this canal would be just as valuable dry as it would be wet, I point ed out that there never would be any vessels to navigate it and if it was to be used at all it would have to be used for some other purpose than a canal. What moved the government to undertake this is more than I can understand. We know that prior to 1904 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) ran in the county of Durham as a Liberal candidate and he had a mouth for the Trent Valley canal in that county and another mouth at Port Hope or some place else. It would appear that one of these mouths must have got lost and that it travelled up the Trent Valley canal and got into Lake Simcoe and in searching for an outlet it happened to discover the mouth of the Holland river and it dug itself into the bank and that was the end of it. If the expenditure on this work were trifling it would not require so much attention from parliament, but when there is $1,000,000 to be wasted it is time for hon. gentlemen to enter a protest and to declare that it would

be in the interests of the country to cut out this appropriation altogether. Many years ago the Trent Valley canal proper- of which of course the Holland river scheme is no part at all-was undertaken by the country and both parties were committed to it. The Minister of Eailways has told us this afternoon that when the Trent Valley canal is completed it will serve as useful a purpose to Canada in carrying the grain trade of the west as the Erie canal does in the state of New York. I hope that is true, and if it be true, then it behooves the minister to use every available dollar he can get for the completion of the Trent canal instead of squandering the money in this Holland river ditch. Those who are conversant with the Trent Valley canal project know it is intended to connect the Georgian bay and the great lakes with Lake Ontario and if that canal can be made a useful factor in the great transportation problems of this country then we would be justified in building it, and in completing it at the earliest possible moment. Instead of wasting the money in this useless Holland canal project it might far better be expended in securing an outlet for the Trent Valley canal either- on. the east or on the west. We know that so far nothing has been done between the Sim-coe lake chain and the Georgian bay at the westerly end, and neither has anything been done as far as I know in opening out into Lake Ontario at the eastern end, so that at the present moment although we have spent millions of money upon the Trent canal it is practically useless for the great purpose for which it was designed. I think it was commenced in the wrong way in the first place. I think it should have been commenced from either the easterly end or the westerly end, but whatever may have been the mistakes of either or both governments in the past it is the duty of the present Minister of Eailways to complete that canal at the first moment the finances of the country will permit. It is his duty now to stop construction upon this useless Holland river undertaking and to open up either the easterly or the westerly end of the Trent Valley canal proper. We know that the government is spending large sums of money at Tiffin, and at Midland and at other Georgian bay ports, so that large steamers can convey the grain trade of the west from the head of the lakes to these ports. In the fall the elevators at these poits will be filled with grain and we knew that ir the rush season there are not sufficient facilities to transport that grain to the sea-board. We know that if the Tient Valley canal proper were completed vessels could load at Tiffin and Midland and other ports so as to relieve the pressure at the elevators and allow the grain to move expeditiously. Looking at it from that Mr. WEIGHT.
standpoint and realizing the necessity for completing the Trent Valley canal at the first moment possible I deprecate this useless expenditure of money on the Holland river. Every one in that section of the country knows that it is an absolute waste of public money to construct this canal in the first place, and that its upkeep will entail a future waste of money for all years to come. If the Minister of Eailways and his predecessors had considered carefully all the conditions surrounding this Holland river canal there would have been no necessity to discuss the water supply because the canal never would have been undertaken. I do trust that the government, even at this late date, will take the money that it is intended to waste on this ditch and put it into the Trent Valley canal proper so that it may be completed and available for the accommodation of the trade of the west. Again I deprecate the hiding of this vote for the Holland river under the general vote for the Trent canal, because there are members in this House who would wish to continue the Trent Valley canal but whot at the same time desire to stop this wasteful expenditure on the Holland river. In conclusion I enter my most vigorous protest against the carrying on of this useless work.

The various speakers impressed upon the government the advantages the improvement would bring to the large and populous district which would be given the boon of competition in rates by water carriage. I have no knowledge of what then took place or of what considerations moved the government of that day to recommend the undertaking of this work, but that recommendation was made to parliament during that session, before I was a member, and parliament passed a resolution devoting an amount of money, to this project. The House of Commons at subsequent sessions provided from year to year for that work by voting additional sums to carry it on. There has not been any occasion, during the time I have been a member of this House, for me to. speak on the subject by way of defending or supporting a proposition to appropriate money for this work, but if there had been, I should have been very ready at any time to do so because I am satisfied that this is a work for the benefit particularly of the riding I represent and which will also be for the general advantage of the rest of Canada, indirectly it is true, but in the same sense as any similar work is an advantage to the whole country.
A good deal of joking has been indulged in with regard to the possible insufficiency of the water supply for the canal when constructed. I stated practically everything I had to say on that point when addressing the Committee of the Whole House three weeks ago. It is an engineering question, of which I know nothing. If I were to sit down and examine for hours the reports of the engineers I should know no more about it when I finished than when I began. All I know is that two or three -years ago, when the first hint of insufficiency of water was made in a newspaper, I asked my old friend Mr. Butler, as an engineer, whether there could be any question in that connection. He said there was none and I have relied with perfect confidence on that opinion 'from that dav to this. I do not suppose that Mr. Butler made personal examination, no doubt he relied on the reports of the engineers who made such examination, but I do suppose that he applied to those Teports his knowledge as an engineer of Mr. AYLESWORTH.
eminence and experience and that, speaking from the facts those reports disclosed, he was in a position to say that there is no question about the sufficiency of the water supply. I am content certainly to rest upon that, and I do not think the hon. gentleman could find any better foundation for an opinion on a subject of that character.
With regard to the benefits which this work will give to the people, in the first place, of the immediate locality, and through them to people who are further 'away, it seems to me that the considerations which have been advanced in general terms by my hon. colleague, the minister in charge of the department, ought to be satisfactory and conclusive. I suppose that for every one there is no place like home.
I suppose that every member of this House thinks his own constituency is the finest.
I certainly have that opinion of mine. When I was a younger man, I used to think that nowhere in this country were farms to be found equal to those of Ernesttown and the Fredericksburghs and Adolphustown. I have changed my mind since, and I say-speaking with as much knowledge in a general way of the province of Ontario as any man here-I do not believe there is any section of the province of Ontario or of the whole of Canada, in which superior farms, better farm buildings, or more prosperous, thriving farmers are to be found than in the county of North York. If this constituency is one in which prosperity abounds, if it is a fine agricultural country and has the advantage of manufacturing establishments, the equals at least of those which any other community of the same size enjoys, what reason is there, when the advantage of water communication can be secured to the heart and centre of that territory by the digging and widening of a stream for a distance of some three or four miles, why that should not be done?
But the question to-day is not whether or no this work should be undertaken. The question before the House is ought we to discontinue it? Should we, by adopting the resolution proposed, condemn the government of four years ago and of to-day for recommending the undertaking of this work? Ought we now to abandon the work and lose the amount of money we have put into it? Facing that question and with the necessity of saying by our vote whether or not we want to censure the government and abandon the work which has been undertaken and upon which a large amount of money has been spent, I cannot see how any hon. gentlemen can hesitate to vote against the resolution. We have undertaken this work, we have committed ourselves to it, we have no reason to doubt that it will be efficient when competed, and we have as satisfactory reasons for believing that it will be beneficial to the community in which it is situated and, through that community, indi-

rectly to the remainder of the country, as we have with regard to any other commercial undertaking which this country is now concerned in as a public work. I can understand the local jealousy which might cause people, who reside at some little distance, to think that their own personal "peculiar interests would be injured by the completion of this work and to seek to prevent its completion. But when we are told that nothing of that kind exists, that it is absurd to suppose there is any kind of local jealousy on the part of the great city of Toronto, into which millions of the people's money have been poured in the past and to which the voters and ratepayers of North York have contributed their full quota, I cannot see why this enterprise should be singled out as one to be condemned and abandoned when I am convinced, oh the reports of scientific men and tny knowledge of the local conditions, that it will be of great benefit to the people of Ihat locality and through them to the people of the whole surrounding country.

Mr. Speaker, this question has been before the House in several forms during the present session. Objection has been taken to the form in which the vote for the Trent Valley canal appears in the estimates. The vote is in one lump sum of $1,000,000 without division. That matter has been briefly referred to by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright). I think that his ground is well taken; for we find that in the Supplementary Estimates, for instance, there is a vote for the Prince Edward Island Railway-a vote relating to this same Department of Railways and Canals-but it is divided into items with the amount specified for each. Throughout these estimates from end to end, we find the same form quite common. But, whenever there is a high-smelling item that is to be carried through, it is always coupled with two or three others and we are asked to swallow the pills, box and all. Many hon. members of this House support the continuation of work on the Trent Valley canal but they would like to see some effort made to complete the system, and are not satisfied with the prospect held out that our children's children and not they will pass by this outlet into Lake Ontario or Georgian bay. And of those that favour expenditure on the Trent Valley canal, many are prepared to vote down this expenditure on the Newmarket canal. The Minister of Railways and Canals, in his effort to defend a very bad case, has wandered far afield. He has quoted masses of statistics showing the number of canals to be found in the older countries of Europe, but he forgot to say that eighty per cent of those canals were built long before the days of railways, and that since the advent of railways very few small canals of
this description have been constructed. Any one who knows anything about the United States knows that canals of this kind were built through Pennsylvania and Maryland years ago, and you can see them there now choked with weeds and unused because the work for which they were designed is now better done by the railways.
Let me point out where this Newmarket canal is and what it is. One has only to look at the map to see where Lake Simcoe is. Lake Simcoe lies at an altitude of about two hundred feet above Lake Ontario. Of course, it has a natural basin with its own drainage system on all sides, and it empties into the Georgian bay by way of the Severn river. A number of small rivers empty into Lake Simcoe from the south. The greatest of these is the Holland river, and, a few miles from its mouth, the Holland river branches into what is called the east branch of the Holland river. The Black river runs a few miles to the east and empties into the lake at Jackson's point. Each of these rivers covers, in its course, a distance of from ten to twenty miles, and, at one time, they were navigable for two or three miles from their mouths for canoes and the batteaux used by the Hudson Bay Company and the settlers of the old days. Each river has its source from a height of from thee hundred to six hundred feet above the level of Lake Simcoe, making the fall in a distance of from ten to twenty miles. The Holland river rises only a few miles from Wilcocks lake, the source of the Humber. The east branch of the Holland river, from about Newmarket, runs through its own valley, and, to reach the main river from Newmarket westward you have to overcome a rise of probably 150 feet. To reach the Black river on the east side you would have to cross another divide about equally high. So, the only territory tributary to the east branch of the Holland river, lies along the Northern Railway. The drainage area of the branch of the river is stated at 61 square miles, which means, roughly, a territory ten miles by six. All the figures given us by the hon. minister relative to the tonnage of the county of York has no bearing on the question, because this tonnage nearly all travels in a different direction. That in the valley of the Holland river travels to the Canadian Pacific Railway and down to Toronto by Kleinburg. That on the east side goes to Toronto by the valley of the Don over the old Midland railway. None of that tonnage could be brought to this waterway because of the expense. The greatest extent of country to be served would be twenty miles by six miles.
I have been at great pains to go through the papers relating to this matter and learn why this ditch was begun. A petition

was presented-no date given-signed by several gentlemen. One bon. member who spoke said that it had been signd by gentlemen in North York. A number of those who signed it were from Barrie and other places. And what did they ask? Simply for the dredging of the mouths of the Black river, the Holland river and the East branch as far as Holland Landing to clear out the weeds and allow the barges that come through the Trent Valley canal system to go to Holland Landing, for their cargoes. In other words, they asked that these places be made harbours, like Barrie. Jackson's Point, or Beaverton, and not that a canal should be built. The section between Cook's bay and Newmarket is ten 'miles. From Holland Landing to Newmarket four and a half miles-the latter is all the country that has need of canalization. That is all that is to be covered by the canal. The rest is merely clearing out silt, and dredging out sand bars and other obstructions. But now, let us see the genesis of this work. The first mention of this canal was immediately before the election of 1904. Some time in October, 1904, Mr. Walsh, an engineer of the department, was hurriedly called from Orillia to that section of country to make a survey of this particular branch. There is a considerable vote around Newmarket and Holland Landing He had to ascertain if something could be done to make a canal or bring about the building of some public work there. Mr. Walsh goes down to that country, and in a few days every loose fish in Newmarket is driving stakes and eating his dinner at the country's expense.
By the way, it was just two or three weeks before the election, and every voter that could possibly be put to work was put to work on the job, and within a very short time they blew in $25,000 of this country's money in making these surveys. Bear in mind immediately before the election. Now you have the whole secret of the purpose of this canal. It was designed for a political purpose. It was so intended by the then Postmaster General, Sir Wm. Mulock, to enable him to carry that constituency, which was gradually goins? to the bad. Politically we find at the same moment that the hon. gentleman who succeeded him, as Postmaster General, and who is now the Minister of Justice, was carrying on an election down in Durham. The question of the Trent Valley canal was made a burning question in Durham. The hon. gentleman being new to politics, thought that he would enter political life with a bludgeon, and he decided the easiest way to secure a majority of the votes was by offering and promising large public works to his constituents. At the same time a gentleman by the name of R. R.

Gamey appeared in Durham. Apparently there had been some differences of opinion between the Minister of Justice and Mr. Gamey previous to that Durham election, and Mr. Gamey and the present Minister of Justice had it out in East Durham, with the result that Mr. Gamey succeeded in landing his man, and the Minister of Justice was defeated
The next we hear of this work was this great deputation that came down to the government asking to have this work carried on. They found out that although they had got the surveys, the thing was beginning to eret a little cold, either that, or the retirement of the Postmaster General, then the Hon. Mr. Mulock, was in contemplation, and it was necessary to make that riding sure for his successor. The gentleman who was to succeed him did succeed him. Bear in mind that the election was in the fall of 1904, this deputation came to see the government on the 22nd of February, 1905. The agitation was kept up during that whole period until away along in the fall of that year, when, on the 16th of October, 1905, the present Minister of Justice was appointed Postmaster General. It was well known at that time that Mr. Mulock had made himself possibly too busv with the question of public utilities, and that his views along the same lines as those of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) running in parallel grooves, did not meet with the approbation of the leader of this government. He was going to retire. his health being very poor at that time. Subsequently it got better when he became a judge. But this constituency must be kept in a ferment of excitement so that there might be a loyal supporter of the government appointed. The matter was carried on in that way. The Postmaster General, now the Minister of Justice, went up for election on November 22, 1905, against a farmer by the name of McCallum, and in spite of this canal agitation, no work having been done at that time, in spite of the surveys he carried the constituency by a reduced majority of 149. The minister says it is a great Reform riding. It is not a great Reform riding apparently, from that majority. Now, succeeding that, Mr. Walsh was asked to make a report. Mr. Walsh is the engineer of the government, who is apparently ready to make a report on anything at a moment's notice, and so far as his figures in this connection are concerned they are misleading in every respect. I do not think the Minister of Railways and Canals will rise in his place and say to this House that any single figure that has been given by Mr. Walsh to him as the responsible minister in charge of that department, in connection with this work, has been within 200 per cent of what the work actually cost, or of the estimate that was made by the responsible man, Mr. MARCH 23, 1909
