A strange thing in connection with these payments for right of way is that a gentleman named Widdifield appears as a partner in about 50 per cent of the transfers of land made in and around Newmarket for this canal. I am told that Mr. Widdifield is a defeated candidate in that riding and a very close friend of our hon. friend the Minister of Justice. I cannot see why the government could not buy these lands direct from the owners without having a partner appear in all transactions. In addition to the right of way there will be heavy expenditure for bridges. I need not point out that there are steel bridges



in connection with this work. Of these two must be steel swing bridges of 88 feet span each, one of 49 feet and one of 64 feet. Any one who knows anything about steel construction will say that you cannot build a steel swing bridge at less than $500 or $1,000 per foot, and the cost, instead of being the $91,000 in the estimate, would be net far short of $150,000.
Then there are the land damages and the work at Wilcox lake. No one has made an estimate on that work except our good, Christian friend Walsh who says $41,000. Mr. Walsh estimated at $290,000 work which has now reached $900,000 so if he says that this work will cost $41,000, we are safe in saying that it will cost not less than $150,000, which with the land damages to be paid, farms expropriated, &c., will bring the total cost of the conservation up to at least $250,000. That would make a grand total for the work of $1,236,104.55- we will drop the 55 cents for the benefit of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham).
Now let us come to the vital point. The one string harped on by hon. gentlemen; opposite with reference to the canal is the feasibility of this work. Any one who knows anything about engineering will tell you that there is practically no engineering problem that cannot be solved. We all know the point to which engineering science has reached, so that to bring into the argument at all the question of the feasibility of the work is to treat us as a lot of children. The great question should have been, not the feasibility, but the commercial value of the work as a public undertaking.
I have pointed out to you how the various lines of traffic parallel each other in the county of York. I have pointed out that the only basin that could be served by this canal is something like 60 square miles in that portion of York. The distance to be saved is about 4 1-2 miles, because I eliminate from the question the amount necessary to dredge the mouth of the river. It is really the 4 1-2 miles that is costing the $1,000,000, as there is a lift of 45 feet in that distance. I have also considered the tonnage arising in Newmarket. I do not believe there is over 60 tons daily all the year around of tonnage in and out of Newmarket. Of that amount 50 per cent will go south to the city of Toronto and the greater portion of the balance will go north of Newmarket so that the total in and out tonnage of Newmarket on which the freight charges could be reduced by this canal would not amount to 20 tons a day. What would the reduction be on 20 tons a day? You can haul a ton 4 1-2 miles on a wagon for a dollar; that is a fairly good price. Therefore, this canal will at most save the people in the immediate vicinity of Newmarket about $20 a day, and as the Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
canal will be opened for about 200 days in the year the saving would amount annually to $4,000. But, we will give good measure and we will double that amount and we will suppose there is a saving of $8,000 a year to the people of Newmarket and its vicinity.
Now, Sir, if we take the total amount that that canal will ultimately cost and figure it at the rate of 4 per cent., there will be a charge on the people of this country of $40,000 a year. Added to that, at the very lowest estimate there will be a charge of $10,000 a year for the maintenance of the locks and for lock tenders, and you therefore have $50,000 a year that the people of Canada will have to pay by reason of the construction of this canal in order to save $8,000 a year to the people of Newmarket and its vicinity. Does any sane man think that that is a good business proposition? I think political economists would say, considering the conditions of this country at the present time, that if the government proceeds to spend say half a million dollars on any given work it should be ranked as a national enterprise, and before such a work is undertaken it should receive the most careful consideration. The question should be asked: will this work be of such a nature that it will serve the neonle of the country as a whole and not merely the people of a small section? Now, I challenge any man on the government benches to state that the building of this Holland river ditch will cheapen by the smallest fraction of a cent the cost of hauling grain from the wheat fields of the west to the sea-board. As a matter of fact the direction of the canal is north easterly, and as everyone knows the traffic of the west would naturally seek the opposite direction as an outlet. The one million dollars which this canal is going to cost if spent in carefully devised improvements at the terminals on the great lakes would appreciably reduce the cost of freight and to that extent benefit the farmers of the west and the people of the country generally. The Minister of Justice declared this afternoon that Toronto was jealous of the expenditure of this money in his riding. What nonsense. Why, the aggregate annual business done in that section of the riding that would be served by this ditch would not equal the business done in one city block in Toronto in the course of a year. But, whenever the Holland ditch is mentioned the Minister of Justice flies into a passion, and he seems to think that a political attack is being made on him. Sir, this is not a personal matter; it is a far graver question, of national concern. The Minister of Finance tells us that there is great difficulty in financing on the money markets of the world at the present day, and that there are small clouds

on the financial horizon which forbode danger. That being so, is it wise for us to spend such a vast sum of money for the mere sake of constructing a political work for the benefit of a single minister of the Crown? To my mind the Minister of Justice should be broader; he should not take such a narrow and sectional view of his interests. The Minister of Public Works told us the other night that expenditure was curtailed this year, and that even a great many necessary public works in his riding could not be proceeded with because the country could not afford it. Why does not the Minister of Justice try to get into the same frame of mind. He cannot; he looks at every thing in a narrow partisan spirit; he is like the man who lived all his life in a political barrel and knows nothing except what he sees through the political bung hole. Let me urge the government once and for all to stop operations on this canal. We have been told that the country is committed to the project, but what has been done already had far better be lost than that additional useless expenditure should be incurred. Sir, this is a political work and nothing else. It may suit the Minister of Justice in his own particular constituency to have us condemn this work, but I can assure him that if he forces it on the country it will not add anything to his political prestige in the rest of the province of Ontario where public works are urgently needed and with regard to which we have with great forbearance agreed to their postponement for this year. It shall afford me great pleasure to vote for this amendment. A political job costing $5,000 or $6,000 is wrong in principle, but when the cost runs into the millions and when it means a charge of 25 cents on every man, woman and child in Canada, it is a political crime.

I would like to remind the House at this stage that in my opinion this discussion is irregular. The estimates contain item 103 for the construction of the Trent canal, and I find from ' Hansard ' that this item was being discussed before the committee on the second of March, and that it remains open for discussion again when the House is in Committee of Supply. This debate seems to have proceeded so far by consent of both sides but under the circumstances it is irregular. If the House is willing to allow the discussion to proceed I am prepared to submit, but I think it my duty now to remind the House that in my view the procedure is irregular.

I listened with a great deal of attention to the speech of the Minister of Railways and I thought he deserved the sympathy of the House in his laboured attempt to justify 99i
the expenditure on the Newmarket canal. Since the Minister of Railways came to the House I have always admired him for the candid manner in which he has given us information and for the frankness with which he has discussed questions relating to his department. But to-day we witnessed the most laboured effort he has ever attempted here. He has our sympathy as no doubt he has the sympathy of his friends. We have seen in the press of the country amusing cartoons in reference to the Newmarket canal, and the Minister of Justice has been portrayed as pumping water out of a well to furnish the canal with a water supply. I thought at first that was only a joke, but it seems the Minister of Railways takes it seriously and he actually informs the House that it is possible to pump water to supply that canal. It would seem that the hon. gentleman thinks that such will be the ultimate result and that water must be pumped from artesian wells to enable the canal to float anything.
Therefore in his efforts all the way through he had the sympathy of the House. One of my reasons for speaking on this matter is that there is in my riding a canal somewhat similar to the Newmarket canal, that is, the Welland canal feeder. That was originally built for a good purpose: for a good many years it supplied the old Welland canal with water drawn from the Grand river. That continued until the Welland canal reached the Lake Erie level, and from that time it has got its water supply from Lake Erie. That canal feeder extends for twenty or twenty-two miles from Dunnville or Port Maitland on the Grand river to Welland, through a good section of country, with Port Maitland at one end and Port Col-borne dt the other. That is a rather important canal, and one might naturally suppose that it would be of a great deal of service and benefit to the section of country through which it Tuns, but let me tell the hon. minister and this House that apart from the original purpose for which it was built, that of supplying the Welland canal with water, it is of little practical value to the people of that section of country. In fact, it is never used. The Minister of Railways and Canals tells us that he has been told by prominent citizens of Toronto that manufactured goods might be shipped from Toronto to Newmarket, transferred there to the canal, and transported to the Georgian bay. I think every one of us knows that that is absolutely ridiculous. You could not do that and make it pay. I believe that that canal of ten miles or more, which is now being built at a cost of between one and two millions of dollars to the people of this country, will be just as useless when completed, as the Welland canal feeder, for the purposes of transportation. It will be of no benefit whatever to the farmers of

that particular section. The Minister of Railways and Canals tells us of the great extent of the farm products of the county of York. One would suppose that he expected these to be transported over this canal. He could apply the same argument to the counties of Haldimand and Welland through which the Welland canal feeder passes. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there are practically no farm products whatever passing through that canal. A short time ago I put a question on the Order Paper with reference to the Welland canal feeder, asking among other things how many vessels had passed through it during the last five years, and what their tonnage was. ^ The question and the answers were published in the local papers of my county, and created a good deal of amusement, because it was stated that 700 vessels had passed through it in the last five years, when the hon. gentleman would have been nearer the mark if he had said seven. I believe the Newmarket canal will be just as useless to the people of the county of York as the Welland canal feeder is to the people of the counties of Haldimand and Welland for the purpose of transporting farm products or manufactured goods. The day has gone by for little branch canals. They never can be made to pay, because nobody uses them. We want through canals, and as a member of this House I am prepared to support any reasonable transportation project which the government may bring forward; but I am not doing my duty to the people of the county of Haldimand, whom I represent, if I do not on their behalf protest against an expenditure of nearly two million dollars which I believe is absolutely wasted. The people of my county must contribute their portion of that money, and on their behalf.I protest against this expenditure as being unwise and not in the public interest.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I may tell the Minister of Railways and Canals that I am in favour of main canals, and I am in favour of branch canals where there is any possible excuse shown for their construction. What are the facts concerning the Newmarket canal? Newmarket stands at an elevation of 770 feet above sea-level; Lake Simcoe stands at an elevation of 717 feet; so that there is a rise between Lake Simcoe and Newmarket of 60 feet. The distance from Newmarket to Lake Simcoe is 6 -7 miles. The distance from Newmarket to Holland Landing, where navigable water is found is 3 -6 miles; and the country is asked to vote an expenditure for a little canal for this distance, in order in the first instance to secure the election of the then Postmaster General, and later on to secure the patronage for the succeeding Postmaster General, now the Minister of Justice, at a cost of $1,000,000. If this were a through canal or if it Mr. LALOR.
were to connect with a through canal, some excuse might be made for it. We find that grain is brought in transit by rail to the country towns, where it is ground, and then it is sent on to the sea-board on a through rate by train; but there is no such thing as a through rate for part water carriage and part land carriage. If this canal had the excuse of being on a through route, so that the grain could be brought in barges, ground, and then shipped on to its destination on a through rate, there could be some excuse for its construction; but there is no possible excuse for the construction of this canal. In the three and a half miles from Holland Landing to Newmarket there is a rise of sixty odd feet, and the water supply is absolutely inadequate, unless, as the minister suggests, reservoirs are constructed to catch the rainfall, or unless he sets all the boys in the country around pumping water with their house pumps. I know of no expenditure in the country more wasteful than this expenditure. I can direct the minister's attention to a part of the country where he might have a proper expenditure. Balsam lake is 838 feet above sea-level. Extending northward from it is the chain of waters which supply the Trent canal system with water. With one lock at Coboconk, one at Norland, one at Elliott's falls, there would be communication for thirty miles inland. All that thirty miles is a timber and an agricultural country in which the farmers have no proper access to the markets, and there are many more farms along that thirty miles than there are along the three and a half miles between Holland landing and Newmarket. The country along those three and a half miles has two lines of railway, one on one side of that little stream, and one on the other. In fact the distance between the railways in some places and the creek is not much more than the Minister of Railways could have taken in a jump in his young days. There is; no trouble crossing the stream at any time, and both the electric and steam railways are close together so that the people are absolutely served in every respect. If the people of Newmarket want to bring up any logs, they can do so by rail at a through rate, but they cannot bring them partly by water and the rest of the way by rail at any such rate. I venture to say that the hon. minister can take one-tenth part of the sum he admits this Newmarket canal will cost, and with that money have a canal built for 30 miles north of Coboconk and by the construction of a trestle north of Minden to Mountain lake and a dam between Mountain lake and Horseshoe, which would raise the water sufficiently to give 30 miles additional navigation; that by an expenditure of less than $250,000, 60 miles of naviable water could be added to the Trent system, and that would go through a country not served by

any railway or even by a decent wagon-road. There are so many ways in which this money could be better expended that I have never been able to see the first motive for building this Newmarket canal. There is not enough water to feed it and there is no need foil it. Three and a half miles is a short distance from a town to a port, and if Newmarket were to grow in size it would be down to Holland landing in a short time, and there would be no need to bring this canal up to the mill of a strong supporter of the government. For the life of me, I cannot conceive any justification for this expenditure, and I do not see why the present minister is carrying it out. I regret I was not present when he made his explanation, but with all his astuteness I. am satisfied he could not give any justification for this, and I believe that in his heart of hearts, he would be delighted tc see this canal wiped out of existence and no part of its construction proceeded with. But even supposing there is a grain of justification for the construction of this canal, the work should have been delayed until the ends were constructed, or in other words until the Trent canal is completed from the Georgian bay to Lake Ontario. There is| no need for this Newmarket canal. There is no timber on Lake Simcoe to bring to this man's mill and no goods to bring to Newmarket. The canal never should have been begun; but if the government are determined to construct it, its construction should be withheld until the Trent canal is completed from the Georgian bay to the Bay of Quinte. Its construction should also have been given second place to the branch canal I have referred to running up to the lakes in Hali-burton county, where there are thousands of settlers who have to drive miles to the nearest railway and where there are millions of feet of timber which cannot be hauled long distances to railways. This timber is not floatable and can only be got to market when a canal is opened. I trust that the hon. minister will reconsider his decision. In the first place I object to the item appearing as part of the Trent Canal system. That system has enemies enough. It has taken a long time to educate public opinion up to the point of considering the Trent as a useful waterway, but to have the Newmarket canal placed in the estimates as part of the Trent canal is adding insult to injury.
How far is Cook's bay from any other portion of the Trent canal?

The Trent canal runs into Lake Simcoe. That part which is at present constructed runs from Hee<-ley's Falls to Balsam lake which is the height of land and onward down the waters of the Talbot river into Lake Simcoe. It
is further navigable from Lake Simcoe into Lake Couchiching. This million of dollars which is being squandered on this Newmarket canal would go far to open up one of the ends of the Trent canal not yet completed. But in place of doing this and giving the traffic of our great northwest easy access to market, the minister is frittering away the public money on little side issues such as the one under consideration. I would not object if there was any use for this Newmarket canal after it is constructed, but it would pay the government forty times over to take this sawmill of this supporter of theirs for whom they are building this canal, and bring it down to Holland landing rather than squander the public money as they are doing. I give the minister warning that with all his dams and! reservoirs, he will never have sufficient water to navigate this ditch in the summer season; and I trust he will see his way clear, before the item is passed, to withdraw any reference whatever to its being part of the Trent Canal system, and let this item stand distinct under its proper name of the Newmarket canal. It is not a canal, it is not even a decent ditch. In dry seasons, not more than a pail of water a second runs down that stream just below the town, I trust the minister will see his way clear to withdraw this vote.

I am glad to be able to add a few words of protest against this proposed expenditure, because I am thoroughly familiar with the district in which this work is to be built. I should like very much to see the first report advocating this canal and the reasons it gives in favour of the work. With regard to the water supply, I think enough has been said about that, because no man who has been in that country year after year but must laugh at the suggestion that there is to be a supply of water for this canal except by artificial means. But I would not worry much about that, for there will be quite enough water for all the purposes for which this canal will be required. In the sixties, seventies and early eighties, Lake Simcoe presented a very busy sight. Steamers and tugs innumerable were on the lake. Going out at night, during the sawing season you were never away from the sight of a mill, while rafts were constantly being towed about the lake. I have lived there in summer for the last twenty-two or twenty-three years, and have seen the tugs towing the rafts. About fifteen years ago, I and many others witnessed the melancholy sight of the last tug and raft on Lake Simcoe. The logs that had drifted to the shore had been carefully picked up and a raft made, and it was towed to Bradford. Bradford is a very enterprising village, about one-third the size of

Newmarket. It has perfect water communication up the Holland river. There used to be enormous saw-mills there. Logs were towed up that river until there were no logs tributary to Lake Simcoe. The mills were burnt or torn down and the mills at Belle Ewart had been abandoned years before. Not for fifteen years has anything larger than a small gasoline boat gone up to Bradford. For years, as a resident at Roach's point, I used to take a party of youngsters up to Bradford every year to play cricket. There is perfect navigation there, unless the stream is over-grown with weeds. But there is not a stick of merchantable timber on Lake Simcoe. Nor is there a carload of bark. Newmarket has two factories and a tannery and they cannot get a stick of timber or a carload of bark for the factories and tannery from the waters tributary to Lake Simcoe. I am as certain as that I stand here that there will not be a ton of freight offered on this Newmarket canal; the work will be absolutely and entirely useless. There are wharfs on different parts of Lake Simcoe. The old Northern Railway built a very extensive wharf at Belle Ewart. The railway had a very prosperous branch while there was business on Lake Simcoe. When the mills were burned down, the Northern Railway took up its tracks running from Lefroy to Belle Ewart, a mile and a half and abandoned the whaTf. A few years ago, the railway re-tracked that line because large icehouses had been put at Belle Ewart. I do not think there is a more melancholy sight than that one sees when one goes down to the old abandoned wharf there. It has rotted and there is no timber, but the stones are there, and on either side are the wrecks of tugs and boats that plied on Lake Simcoe when business was done there. There are the hulls of five or six tugs and two or three passenger boats. There is only one passenger boat on Lake Simcoe, and it is run because they take excursions now and again in the summer. But there is no business to be done, and not a possibility of any business on this canal. And the expense of it will be about a million and a quarter of dollars. Now, the ministers of this government are trustees for the people, and they are wasting every dollar of the people's money that is put into that canal just as completely as if they threw it into the river; in fact, it would be better for them to take that money and throw it into the Tiver, for that would end the expense, whereas, spending it in this useless canal, there will always be more or less expense of maintenance. I passed that ditch yesterday. I went up to my summer place for the purpose of trying to get the facing for a wharf there-not a wharf for commercial purposes but only for bathing purposes. And I could not get even enough timber there to face that small Mr. OSLER.
wharf thirty feet long. The timber has to be brought from Toronto by rail to build that little bit of a wharf. The wharf that the government built there three or four years ago has been of great service. It i3 spoken of very highly by all the summer outsiders, and I was told yesterday that as many as twelve black bass had been caught by the boys off the end of that wharf last season. The bass are getting very scarce.
By and by they will be gone.

They are nearly all gone now. Bradford is probably a more important point than Newmarket so far as grain is concerned. It is a large grain-buying centre. But the idea of buying grain at Bradford and shipping it by canal never entered the head of any sane man. I think, in all fairness, that a million dollars is a good deal of money, even in flush times. This government did not seem to think so when times were good, but now, I should think with the revenues in a less satisfactory condition, even they would look upon a million dollars as an amount of fair importance. Before spending the money on this work, it would be well to get a business man-not an engineer, he does not report on the business-but get one or two business men to report on the possible business for that canal when it is built. On the trolley cars, going up yesterday, this work was discussed by almost every one, and the general talk among those going in and out of the car was that the work would not go on any further. The thing was a laughing stock; one after another as he came in said, ' Well, I guess that is the last money that will be spent there.' The government will do wisely to have a report from a business standpoint and carefully reconsider their position. Then, let them have the boldness to say that they were mistaken in what they have done and cut it out, because this money will be lost just as surely as it is put into this work
It has often been a matter of remark and wonder that there seems to be so little feeling of the responsibility of trustees on the part of the government in regard to these matters. It has been remarked in my hearing over and over again, and I think it is generally recognized, that there is a great want of the responsibility of trusteeship in our public life. Now how can we expect anything else if the trustees for the government recklessly, deliberately throw away a million or a million and a half of the people's money without the first shadow of excuse for doing so ? I make the assertion that that canal when built will be absolutely useless, that never a ton of freight will go up or go down it. There is one saw-mill, or factory, there, which uses lumber, but it uses nearly all hardwood. Now there is no hardwood on Lake Simcoe

or on any tributary to it, indeed there is no timber of any sort. Even cordwood has reached such a price that it is cheaper for the farmers to pay freight rates on coal. They have to pay now $5.75 a cord for wood. I speak of what I know, and I appeal to the minister and to the government to reconsider this project and to save the country a million dollars.

I wish to say a few words with reference to this before the debate is closed. It seems to me that in considering whether it was wise or not for the government to expend this great sum, they ought to have had some estimate of the tonnage that was likely to be hauled over that canal. So far as regards any information disclosed to this House to-day, we have had no such estimate. No engineer seems to have estimated for the government the amount of freight that is likely to be hauled over that canal. The question was asKed the Minister of Railways, but either he did not deign to give the information, or he did not have it. Now in view of the fact that there was no information, what justification can the Minister of Railways give to the House for going on with such an unwise expenditure ? We ask ourselves, we who have some knowledge of the locality, what kind of trade is likely to spring up? The hon. gentleman behind me (Mr. Osier) said that there will not be a ton of freight carried over it. I would not go that far. There is one grist mill in Newmarket. The time might come when grain would be delivered from the Northwest at Victoria Harbour, and if small boats could go down the Trent Valley canal info Lake Simcoe they could bring a portion of the grain from Lake Simcoe into Newmarket. That is the only way of bringing in freight from the outside. With regard to the possibility or probability of handling the trade of that great and rich county of York, and the Minister of Railways seems to think there was a possibility when he spoke of its immense wealth, I think that might be well left out of the question entirely. Why ? Because the trade of that whole county of York goes to the great city of Toronto on the south, and the canal is away in the north. He said it was likely to cheapen freight rates. How could it cheapen freight rates, how could it come into competition with railways that are carrying trade from that county to-day ? The only way to get trade for the canal would be to go round nearly 200 miles to carry freight that is carried on the railways to-day to Toronto from Newmarket, which is only 25 miles. What kind of competition would you have if you had to carry freight over 200 miles where the railways can carry it only 29 miles ? There would be no competition at all. The thing is so absurd that no one who knows the
geography of the country and the direction of the trade of the country, would consider it for a moment. What other enterprise is it going to serve? Mr. Cane was the man who was chiefly instrumental in getting that enterprise started by the government. I think there is a fatality about it in some way or other, because we are told that he took the contract for dredging at $46,000, and after he had worked at it for a length of time, the contract had to be taken off his hands. The very man that was instrumental above all others in getting the government to build it is the man who is now going to suffer for it, and for what purpose? To bring in logs for his saw-mill From where ? The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) says there is no timber, practically, around Lake Simcoe. He is correct. Forty years ago there was lots of timber, when the ' Emily May ' was running on Lake Simcoe, and the ' Ida Burton ' and other small boats; there was timber all around it. But the timber has all been taken away, and there is no trade left in that line.
But there is one line of commerce that the Minister of Railways did not mention, and only one that is at all probable or possible. That is a trade that was carried on very successfully between thirty and forty years ago by men living on that marsh where this canal is going. What was it ? Catching frogs and sending them down to New York. That trade is going on yet, and there may be some freight carried in that article of commerce. I think it is capable of great development, because that marsh is a very extensive one, it is a marsh where the frogs grow to a very large size, and the business is likely to afford a permanent trade, and the only trade that the canal is likely to find. They used to carry the frogs by stage from Keswick to Newmarket, and ship them from there to Toronto, and thence to New York. Now they can swim the frogs down the canal and take their heads off at Newmarket, and ship them from that place, that will save something in transportation for at least a portion of the distance. That is the only permanent trade that will be found.
Now in regard to the water supply. I have jumped across that creek, I venture to say, hundreds of times-if I said a thousand times, I think I would be within the mark. That will give you some idea of the water supply. The minister said that 507 cubic feet of water passed over that per minute. Where under Heavens did it come from ? I dont know, nor can any man imagine, who has ever lived in that locality. I have lived there, and crossed it a thousand times. When you talk like that, why, it is totally absurd and totally incomprehensible for any one to think of it. It reminds me of a story that was told in the west, when some one was asking

who were the three greatest liars in the world. He said they were in the west, that a certain man was one liar, and he was the other two. I think the Minister of Railways and Canals must be the whole three. He must have had water on the brain, or a very fertile imagination. I say the expenditure of this money cannot be justified. Not only will it be a living monument of folly, but it will stand to the discredit of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and of every hon. member who supports it, and of every one who takes part in the expenditure of that money.
