House in Committee on Bill (No. 79) respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-Mr. W. McIntyre.
On section 1,

That subsection (a) of clause 1 be struck out and the following added as a subclause:
The line of railway described in subsection (a) of section 3, of chapter 74 of the Statutes of 1907, shall be commenced within one year from the passing of this Act, and at least 30 miles of said line shall he completed in each year thereafter until the whole be completed.

As this line of railway, in reference to which the Canadian Pacific are applying for a renewal of its charter, has a direct interest to the people in the district I represent, I wish to strongly support the amendment, which I believe should receive the support of this House. I understand that a similar amendment was suggested in the Railway Committee, but for some reason it was not accepted in that committee. There can be no objection to the passing of this amendment as the Canadian Pacific Railway are in a position, so far as I know, if they have the wish and the will, to commence operations on this branch line of railroad within the next twelve months. Unless it is the intention of the Canadian Pacific Railway to undertake this work in the immediate future, we should not grant an extension of time. Between the main line of the Canadian Northern Railway and the most northern branch of that railway, which ends at the city of Prince Albert, there is a distance of 80 or 85 miles. That section of the country is well settled; every homestead quarter-section is taken up and farmers living in that part of the country are to-day hauling their grain from 35 to 40 miles in order to reach a market. If this branch line of railway from township 32, range 21 or 22, to the city of Prince Albert, Mr. SPROULE.
>
were built, I have every confidence that it would be a paying line of railway, right from the date of its completion. Objection has been taken to the imposing of great restrictions on the granting of these charters. In some cases that argument, I think, is good, but I do not see any reason why we should not place this restriction on the granting of charters to the Canadian Pacific Railway. We know they are in a position financially to construct these branch lines of railroad that are asked for in this Bill. We have evidence of their strong financial position in the recent issue of $50,000,000 of additional capital stock.
I am strong in my support of this amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Rutan) because I have a lurking suspicion _ that the Canadian Pacific Railway do not intend to carry out their proposals as contained in this charter for which they are asking. They have had this charter for the past two years and they have done practically nothing in the way of commencing operations. Why should they seek for a renewal and for an extension of time if they do not purpose going on with the road? The answer to that question is that there is a suspicion in the minds of the people of the constituencies of Prince Albert and Humboldt that the Canadian Pacific Railway's policy is to blanket that territory so as to hamper the construction of branch lines by other railroads. The Canadian Pacific Railway did practicallv no railway construction in northern Saskatchewan until the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific was carried through the central part of that province and then we found the Canadian Pacific Railway pushing forward the construction of their Kirkella line, which, east of Saskat-toon for some 75 miles and for a great many miles west of Saskatoon, parallels the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Just as soon as the Grand Trunk Pacific oorp-menced building the Canadian Pacific Railway got busy with their Kirkella extension. Now, the people of the constituency of Humboldt and of Prince Albert want this branch line constructed from or near the town of Lani"fln in the district of Humboldt to the city of Prince Albert. We have no reason to believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway actually intend to build this line; in fact I have it on good authority that the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway was interviewed recently by some persons who were very anxious to see the road built and he gave no assurance whatever that the company would undertake its construction either next year or in the year following. We have a suspicion, nay we have a belief, that the Canadian Pacific Railway are simply asking for this renewal and extension of time for the purpose of covering that territory by this charter and that being so we ought to insert the restrictions called for by the amendment.

Some may argue that the granting of this charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway does not tend to keep another railroad from building through the same territory but to my mind that is not a convincing argument because, just as soon as another railway obtains a charter through the territory and commences operations the Canadian Pacific Railway is in a position to step in ahead of them and effectually cut off the other company from constructing. We have reason tc believe that a branch line can be obtained from the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific right over this same territory and that aid can be secured for such a branch line from the government of Saskatchewan. But, if this House grants this charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway without restriction as to time, then, just as soon as the Grand Trunk Pacific commences work on the line they might propose to build, the Canadian Pacific Railway can step in and parallel them every foot of the way to the city of Prince Albert. On behalf of the people of those districts who are asking for railroad communication and better transportation facilities I strongly support this amendment. To prove conclusively that the Canadian Pacific Railway are conspiring to blanket that country with these branch line charters I may say that they also have a charter which they obtained through the taking over of the Manitoba and North Western and which enables them to build some considerable distance east of the line for which they now ask an extension of time. That runs through the Fishing Lake country east of the Great Quill lakes and also north easterly to the city of Prince Albert. By another Bill, they are asking for an extension of time on that branch line although they have had that charter since 1893. For 16 years has that charter been in possession of the Canadian Pacific Railway and they have done absolutely nothing to carry out its terms. These two branch line charters into the city of Prince Albert ; the one under the Manitoba-North Western charter and the one contained in this Bill, practically cover the only two available routes into Prince Albert from the south and east, connecting with any of the main lines of the great trunk railways. The fact that they are also applying for an extension of time on this other charter is evidence that they are simply trying to cover this territory by charters so as to prevent any other railroads from being built. On behalf of the people of the constituency I represent and who require this line to be immediately constructed I very strongly support the amendment of the member for Prince Albert.

This question has been raised in the House and in the committees during the last few years, amendments have
been moved on the lines of the present amendment and the whole question has been thoroughly discussed. But, the question for us to consider now is whether any good result is likely to come from the passing of such an amendment and whether if passed it would result in any of these railways being built any the quicker. I suppose there is no member from the north west who has not received constant protests against the renewal of charters, not only of the Canadian Pacific Railway but of the Grand Trunk Pacific branch line company, and of the Canadian Northern Railway Company as well. I have received such protests couched in the very strongest language asking that this parliament should not renew charters unless definite guarantees were given that the lines would be built in the very near future. I have a protest in my hand from a meeting held at a place called Wiggins, Saskatchewan, protesting against the renewal of the charter for the Moosjaw-Lacombe branch, which is included in this clause, and I would ask the Minister of Railways to state whether he has taken any steps to endeavour to remedy the grievance which the people of Wiggins feel they are suffering under ; whether he has approached the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and asked them whether they are prepared to undertake the building of this branch in the near future, and whether he has used any argument with them to induce them to do so. I think it is up to the Minister of Railways to show that he has taken some such step. There is no doubt that the people of that section of country are suffering under a great sense of injustice in having been induced to settle in that country far away from the railway. The government is in a position, in dealing with the three great companies that have lines in the Northwest, to bring some pressure to bear upon them to build branch lines where they are most needed. For instance, in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, we have been informed that the government have given their consent to the issue of common stock by the company at a rate which is generally (conceded to be far below its Teal value. That, I take it, is a concession to the company, and when these great companies come to the government asking for concessions, the government have it in their power to endeavour by negotiation to induce them to give something in return. I would therefore ask the Minister of Railways whether he has had a protest from Wiggins, the one which I have in my hands states that a similar one ha3 been addressed to him- -and whether he has taken any steps to endeavour to procure for these people the building of the railway , which, no doubt, they were promised in the

past, and which, it is to be hoped, they will receive at some time in the near future.

I wish to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan). That hon. member and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), the two members representing the people in that part of the country through which this short line of about 130 miles will run, should be in the best position to know whether this charter should be renewed or not. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat says that it is a question whether the passing of such an amendment will increase the building of railroads in the country. Perhaps it may not; but speaking from the experience of my own district, I can say that where we cannot get the roads built, the people are unanil mously in favour of the charters not being renewed; and if the representatives from that part of the country who know what the people want, ask for a certain thing, I think it is up to this House to pass the amendment they propose.

I also agree with the previous speakers to this extent, that I think the government and this House ought to exercise serious control over the great roads in the west. It is a fact that there are large districts there which have no railroads, and the people in those districts are very anxious to have railroads; but it is also a fact that the great railroad companies, instead of devoting their attention mainly to giving to the people the accommodation they require, are engaged largely in a kind of strategy one against the other. I contend that the Minister of Railways has sufficient power to control the situation, and if he exercised that power he would see that none of the plans of these railroads which are for the mere purpose of strategy should be approved of while roads which are necessary for the settlers are not being built. The government should see that the funds of these companies are not wasted in building parallel lines merely to compete with existing lines. That is not opening up the country; it is only enabling these companies to play a game the one against the other. It is time that all that was stopped, and that any money which any of these companies have for the construction of new lines should be applied in opening up roads in new districts and giving a service where there is none at the present time.

I am surprised at the action of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan) and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neelv), and I might say the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). A few days ago when we had another question similar to the present one before the committee, an amendment was moved by my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Glen Camp-Mr. LAKE.
bell) to compel a railroad company to build 25 miles of road during the first year. That amendment was carried by the committee, though it was opposed by all of these gentlemen. The very same arguments which are put forward to-night in support of this amendment were put forward at that time by the hon. member for Dauphin and myself in support of the amendment he moved, with regard to the Winnipeg and Northwestern Railway Company. That company had four or five alternative routes, practically blanketing the whole country. The hon. member for Dauphin had petitions from every municipality in his district, asking the government not to grant an extension to the company without compelling it to build a certain number of miles every year. We carried that view in the committee, but when the Bill came before the House the gentlemen promoting it had it referred back to the committee, and it became practically a political question. Every hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House was arrayed against the amendment, and defeated it, though it was entirely similar to the amendment moved to-night. Consistency ought to be the rule of this House, and I am surprised that a member can take one attitude in the committee and an entirely different attitude in this House. I have no brief from the Canadian Pacific Railway; I have no reason for having a brief from that company. In my own county the Canadian Pacific Railway Company last fall stopped work on a Tailroad which was very much needed, and just in the midst of the political campaign, allowed my opponent, assisted I believe by the Canadian Pacific Railway engineers, to put on a large staff of men in the effort to compass my defeat. I mention this to show that I have no brief from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I would like to see consistency in the House, and I am not prepared to support this amendment because I believe that the men who have moved as they did in the committee and did not succeed do not deserve any better success on the floor of the House.

I am not going to detain the House at any length. I simply want to bring to its attention the fact that various gentlemen who have spoken tonight have shown the utmost inconsistency. I am not going to refer to the other Bill, which has been referred to by my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), further than to say that it seems with certain members in this House, to make a very great difference whose ox is gored. Those same gentlemen took a very prominent part in fighting against the wishes expressed in the petition of the men who sent me down here to represent them, and then they ask us to pay some attention to what their own people want. I wish to point out that it is certainly the people of the districts

through which these railways are to run, who should know what they want, and they have expressed, through their representatives in this House, what they do want. They want railways, but they strongly object to charters lor hot air lines being granted, and long experience has given them good reasons for their objection. These charters have done more to retard settlement than anything else, and it is but right that this committee should pay attention to such expressions of opinion, coming from the people who are directly interested. If the Canadian Pacific Railway intend to build those branch lines, it is no great hardship to ask them to show their good faith by building 20 or 30 miles the first year. The committee should certainly pay great attention to the message sent them from Prince Albert'.
It is easy for my hon. friends to ask this government to straighten out all these things.
This is the place.

There is a place called the Railway Committee where attention should be paid them. We have a duty to perform as representatives as well as members of the government. I shall not have to make any apologies for the position I take on this Bill because I have taken it on other Bills as well. I take it that what the petitioners want in these various localities is a railway as speedily as possible. I may be wrong, but in my opinion to pass an amendment in this line will rather injure than hasten the prospects of getting that road. To say to the Canadian Pacific Railway that they must construct so many miles this year is only repeating in another way what we do say in their charter, and that is that they must begin operations in two years and build in five. If this amendment were going to hasten the building of the railway, it would be different, but it is more likely to defeat the object which hon. gentlemen have in view. This question does not come up only in the renewal of this charter but comes up regularly in the railway committee in the renewals of many charters. To place a clause of that kind in the charter would simply mean that these people would be back sooner for another renewal. If they are ready to construct the line, and if it be in their interest to do so, they will construct. But if we put in a more stringent clause, it will mean that the Canadian Pacific Railway will not build any more quickly but will come back in twelve months instead of two years, and ask for a renewal. Our object is to get railways into these parts of the territories that are not now served by them. I understand thoroughly, as the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has said, that there are many instances where these companies spar for situation or location, not having, for the time being, any great desire to build, but rather to. keep some other line from building; but on the whole, the course we have pursued has been reasonably successful in getting lines built as rapidly as settlement required. It is a fact that many people have gone into remote parts of the west, and are in very needy circumstances so far as railway lines are concerned. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) handed me a petition, of which I think, I had already received a copy. My usual plan, on receiving a petition, is to make an extract from it and call the attention of the railway company concerned to the fact that I have received it, and urge them to do everything to grant the prayer of the petitioners. Suppose we put the provision asked for into this charter, we will have to put it into every charter for a branch line in the Canadian Pacific Railway. But it is impossible for any railway company to cover all the territory which requires a railway. It stands to reason that where the most people are found, the greater necessity exists and the greater traffic there will be for the line, and it is natural for a railway company to build where it will get the most traffic. Consequently, the places most needing railways will get them first. I am anxious to see this line extended, but I do not think the placing of this in any charter will help one iota to get a railway constructed but will rather have the opposite effect. In the Railway Committee, I have taken that ground. I have asked the committee on several occasions not to place such a clause in the Bill and I must ask the Committee of the Whole House to take that ground. I make that request in order to be consistent and for the further reason that I do not believe that the insertion of such a provision in any charter will facilitate the building of the road but will rather retard it.
Amendment negatived.

I beg to move that letter G, clause 1, be struck out. This letter G refers to a short line of about 100 miles from the town of Estevan in a northwesterly direction. I am not going to ask this House to put in a clause providing for the building of 25 miles this coming year, simply because my experience during the past five years makes me understand thoroughly that it will not be carried. But I believe that I represent absolutely the views of the people in that part of the country where this charter exists, and consequently I move that that clause be struck out alto-

gether and the charter cancelled. If we cannot have a railway built in the near future, we do not want that charter on our statutes, because, so long as the charter is there, the Canadian Pacific Railway will not take any steps to go on with the building of the line, but will stand as a block in the way of others building it. That country has been settled the last 18 or 20 years and well settled, and the farmers there have to draw their wheat from 30 to 40 miles, if they draw it to a Canadian town and 10 to 20 miles if they draw it to the American town of Ambrose, in North Dakota. Last year, about 150,000 bushels of wheat was drawn from that comer of my constituency into North Dakota and shipped over the Jim Hill system. As I have said before, I want the Minister of Railways and the government to understand that unless some change is made in the handling of these railway companies, unless they are ocmpelled to do better in the future than they have in the past, the strongest effort will be made on the part of the people in the southern portions of Alberta and Saskatchewan to have the Hill system brought into the country. And if conditions continue as they are, while I should be sorry to see the traffic go out of the country and through the United States, yet, I, for one, wiM welcome any change in the state of affairs, and I know that ninety-nine, if not one hundred per cent of the people I represent will take the same position. I know, also, that in asking the committee to strike out that clause I am representing faithfully and correctly the views held by my constituents. And whose views should carry in this matter-the views of the Canadian Pacific Railway who have had charters for fifteen or twenty years for roads which they have not built, or the views of the farmers? Whose views should we in this committee consider? I am not asking for any favour of building twenty-five miles a year, but I am asking that that clause be struck out, so that other companies may be given an opportunity to come in and build these railways.

I would support, as I did last year, the motion to place in all charters and all renewals of charters provisos that a railway company should commence to build its line within a reasonable period of time. But I do not think it is quite right to make exceptions in these matters.
I am not asking to have any of the other charters interfered with. This is the only one in which I am asking to have this clause dropped, and the Bill we are discussing now covers othei branches.
That is just the case; the hon. gentleman is asking that the renewal of one particular charter be refused.
Yes.

Thus making an exception in that case. I think we should treat all cases alike. The hon. gentleman has taken very strong ground with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but that is the only company we ever heard him speaking against in connection with these matters.

That is the only one in
my constituency.

Only last year the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company, asked for a renewal of their charter, a charter given them three years before, blanket-ting an immense area of country for the construction of branch lines, not a single one of which had they started to build. Yet this House decided that their charter was to be renewed. I do not think that we should make fish of one and fowl of another. Until this House decides, as I think it ought to decide, that a provision shall be put in all charters requiring the company to begin and complete its work within a reasonable time, I think we should go on as we have gone on in the past, practically allowing free trade in charters.

It is somewhat amusing to me to note how jealous the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is of his own We have been fighting in the committee and in the House for just what he proposes in this particular case-we have asked that no charter should be renewed except on the condition that the company shall construct a certain portion of the line within a certain time. We had a case of this kind before the committee a short time ago and got such a provision put in the Bill. And what did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) do? He got up at the next meeting and asked to have the Bill reconsidered, and then we found him voting down the amendment we had already carried in the committee. He seeks to make that limit in his own constituency. But the Bill I have just referred to related to my constituency. I am quite willing to guard the interests of his constituents, but I would like him to reciprocate by assisting us who are just as anxious as he is to have railways constructed to serve our people. The hon. gentleman is very emphatic in that. He wants to get on the floor and make a little spiel that it may go to his constituents showing how strong he is on this subject. I am prepared to support the hon. gentleman notwithstanding his attitude on the general question.

The hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff) and some other hon. members of this House, myself included, are charged with inconsistency in the position we take on, this charter and on a certain other charter that came before the Railway Committee and before this House some time ago. So far as I am concerned, I do not feel that charge. I do not intend to speak for the hon. member for Assini-boia or the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan) or any other hon. member. But it seems to me that every case ought to be taken on its individual merits. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) knows that this is not a similar case to the other.
Explain the difference.

The hon. gentleman knows that the Canadian Pacific Railway is in a position financially to go ahead with the, construction of these branch lines for which they are asking extension of time. He knows that they could, within twelve months, build twenty-five miles on these branch lines if they wished to do so. But he knows that in the other case referred to, the company was not in a position to go ahead. If any leniency is to be shown, it ought to be shown to new companies, for they have their organization to complete, their financing to do, and other preliminary work to get through with. But the Canadian Pacific Railway has its main lines constructed and also has money to build these branch lines. The cases are not parallel, and the charge of inconsistency made by the hon. member for Macdonald and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) are not well founded.
Amendment (Mr. Turriff) negatived.
On section 2,

I would like to have an assurance from the minister that he will give the people ample time to be heard before he accepts the route laid down by this company. There was an amendment passed in committee in reference to this clause, we inserted the words ' High river ' in the charter. I would like the minister to consider the distance these people are from the head office at Ottawa, and that he will allow them, I should say, thirty days. It is sometimes important that these people should have ample time to take these things into consideration. I think the minister told the committee they would have at least two weeks. I would like an assurance that they will get ample time.

I would not like to be put in a position to define ample time. We always give sufficient time, or what we think is sufficient time for all parties to be heard. That is the rule of the department. My hon. friend says thirty days. It strikes
me that would not be necessary. However, we will telegraph to the people in those localities that we are going to have a hearing at such a date, perhaps a little less time than he mentions. However, we will see that they get adequate time.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
House Tesumed debate on motion to go into Committee of Supply and the amendment thereto.

I want to say a few words on this motion before it comes to a vote. Primarily the motion affects the locality in which the work is situated, but it is that kind of a motion which I think, if we are attentive to our duties and mindful of our responsibilities, challenges the attention of every member who has a seat in this House. It is a case of the expenditure of a million dollars of the public money for a work in a locality the grounds for which are altogether inadequate. The discussion well illustrates three positions: First, the way in which the money is sometimes appropriated-I wish I could say 'sometimes,' I think I ought to say in which the money is very frequently appropriated by this government; in the second place, it is illustrative of the way, after the money is placed in the hands of the responsible ministers, it is used for the work; and lastly, it has been illustrative of the methods by which ministers undertook to defend, if you can call it a defence, a vote of this kind, appropriated in this way, and carried out as this has been carried out. Now I made a motion for the papers, and one of the cardinal points I made in that motion was this: I asked for all reports, or papers, or documents which had regard to the commercial foundation of the transaction. After all, ought that not to be the basis and the beginning of the whole thing? Surely it is not enough to say that you will appropriate money because an engineer tells you that what you want to build is feasible and can be properly built? The foundation of the whole thing is this: Is it a necessary or an advisable work? Is it in the interest of the development and commerce of the trade of the country; and if it is not a military necessity, if it is not a national necessity, there is no other ground upon which to place it than that it is a work necessary and advisable, and for which that amount of money is not too much to appropriate. Now, when these papers were brought down, what did I find? -or rather what did I not find? I did not find one syllable from the beginning of the papers to the end showing any attempt by anybody to find out whether there was a commercial basis for this transaction, not one. The only thing that is given with reference to the commercial side of it, if you
Did you ever see the creek?

I have looked for the creek but I have not seen it yet. Now, as to the engineering part of this work, I ask the Minister of Railways if under the circumstances surrounding it he thinks this House or the country can have any confidence in his enginering department. What are the facts? The canal is divided into two sections and one section takes you from Lake Simcoe to Holland Landing, that being the improvement of a waterway and not the building of a canal. That is the first /Sedtion, and the one which one would suppose it would be economical to build first. But what happens: the Minister of Railways sent his engineer and told him to make his examination and give an estimate
what it would cost to put it in shape and the engineer gave him an estimate of $46,000 and the contract was let for $46,000. For two years the contractors held that work and did absolutely nothing. Under what rule did the department leave that work in the hands of the contractors-some of them their own friends and very near and strong friends and influential in the constituency-by what rule were thev en-

abled to hold that for two years without doing any work? The contractors had a pumping machine, the engineer was on the ground, he had no faith in the machinery from the first. After the contractors had been at it a year and done practically nothing he wrote to the department that he had no more faith in the machinery and their capability of doing the work than he had a year before and yet the work remained in the contractors' hands, they doing nothing. But the gravamen of the charge against the railway department is that when it came to a second letting of the contract and the making of the second estimate, the engineer of the department estimated the work to be worth not $46,000 but $131,000. What reliance can we place on the engineers of a department who will take the very same piece of work under the very same conditions, with a lapse of two years, and make such a difference in the estimate. But up to this date not a stroke of work has been done on this initial part of the undertaking. That was dredging work and nothing could work on it but a dredge and the few men engaged on the dredge. It did not distribute the patronage sufficiently and the election was coming on in October, and instead of going on with the first part of the work the department gave their energies to the second part of the work where they could multiply the employment of men and teams and spend $150,000 or more during the few months preceding the elections. What happened? The minister's engineer made the first estimate of the cost of the whole canal at $291,000, and that was the estimate we had when we first voted money for this; in fact I think we were told it would cost less. A little while after the engineer made another estimate and it came up to about $328,000; he afterwards made another estimate of the whole thing, and it came up to $354,000, and a short time afterwards another engineer of that department went on the very same ground and put on it an estimate of $596,826. How are we to reconcile operations of that kind with a well conducted department and a competent set of engineers. Tenders were called for and the lowest tender was $652,000 and the contract was let at that price, which was $50,000 or $60,000, more than the estimate. And now, at the very last we have dragged out of the department that this work which at first was to cost about $300,000, entered into by parliament on an estimate of $291,000-is now estimated to cost about $970,000, not taking into consideration the water conservation which is necessary, and which will bring the total cost up to about $1,200,000. In that way we were led by misrepresentation, absolute misrepresentation, and whether by the engineer or the minister matters very little to this House. I challenge Mr. FOSTER.
any man to show a business foundation for that undertaking. What does it mean ?	$1,200,000 taken out of the people's taxes and put into that place, when all over this country men are starving for railroad facilities in the west and in the east, and cannot get a dollar for development because of such expenditures as this. The other day, in the far east, a much desired and long promised bit of railway was pleaded for by members on both sides of politics. It would cost altogether some $300,000 or less. What was the plea for not building that railroad? 'These are times of financial stress; we have not the money, and we cannot go on with the work.' To-day we have coming from every portion of the great northwest, where the hardy sons of the older provinces and the men we have invited from other countries have gone and taken their lives in their hands, and with their small families have settled in advance of the great lines of transport, appeal for transport facilities; and you tell them that you cannot raise the money to subsidize railways; but you can find a million dollars to put into a ditch at the request of our Minister of Justice who must be buttressed by things of that kind. How much is there to be done in this country? What forest conservation is there staring these men in the face, and how little are they doing to come up to their responsibilities in that respect; it cost money; but a million dollars can be found to put into this place in North York, and the Minister of Justice has nothing better as a plea than to say, "with his accustomed modesty, that he does not want to take the credit of having originated the work, but he would be proud if he could take that credit, and anyway he stands up for it.
Mr. Speaker, I only wish we could have in these galleries the taxpayers from every part of this country, to listen to this discussion of what I am sorry to say is but a sample of the many ways in which their money is wasted. We are not charging any graft; we are not charging any dishonest work in the department or with the contractors in this case. There may be graft; we do not know it, and we are not charging it. This case rests entirely on its business merit. It is cheap logic, very cheap logic, for the Minister of Justice to try to turn the point when the argument is against him, by saying that it is the jealousy of other constituencies, or party zeal, that is urging this discussion. For my part, party does not enter into it, nor do I believe that it does in the case of other gentlemen who have spoken on the subiect. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is painful, absolutely painful, to see the waste of money in such a place and on such a construction and to see it going through this House apparently

treated in a spirit of light comedy by the responsible minister, and with absolute indifference by the other ministers of the Crown. Will any of them stand up and give us a reason for it? Let them show to the representatives of the taxpayers, who if not here to-night, may hear something of this by the only voice we have to reach them, the voice of the press, how they can justify this expenditure. We have dug things out in the province of Quebec that have been shameful, in the Public Works Department and in other departments; we have dug things out in other provinces which have been shameful; but for sheer, wanton, absolute waste, I do not know anything that equals this case of a million dollars of the people's money thrown into a profitless ditch.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, in the course of his observa-vations, did me the honour of saying that he would like to know what was passing in my mind when I was listening to the debate. I am glad on this occasion to be able to gratify the curiosity of my hon. friend. What was passing in my mind, when I was listening to my hon. friend and to some of his associates, was that this motion was a fair sample of how scandals are manufactured.
I am sorry that you had not anything better than that running in your head.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To-morrow we shall have in the press the speech of my hon. friend, the gist of which, coming after the other speeches to which we have listened, is that the government are corruptly spending $1,000,000 for the purpose-to use the elegant language of my hon. friend- of boosting a minister of the Crown.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am glad to find that I interpret correctly the sentiment that prevails on the other side of the House. This is the reason we have now another scandal. The scandal in this instance is that we are spending $1,000,000 for the purpose of boosting a minister of the Crown. The minister of the Crown at that time was a gentleman who was much respected in this House while he was here, and who is much respected in the position he now occupies-Sir Wm. Mulock. For my part, I do not believe that any man in Canada who knows Sir William Mulock will believe that he ever tried to encourage any work in his constituency for the purpose of boosting his own nolitical fortunes. I think the reputation of Sir William Mulock is above any aspersion that can be cast against him by my hon. friend or anybody else. I think his reputation is above any such argument, if I can dignify anything of that kind by calling it an 100
argument. But, Sir, how did we come to undertake this work? If it was for the purpose of boosting the election of my friend and colleague at the time, Sir Wiliam Mulock, how was it that it was the opponent of Sir William Mulock who came here and asked the government to undertake this work? My hon. friend said, in almost the last words he pronounced, that he would be glad if we had in this room the taxpayers of the country to see how their money was wasted. Why, Sir, if there is any wasted money in this instance, it was at the instance of the taxpayers of this country. We had a delegation here of the sound electors, the best men in the riding of North York. We had the mayor of the town of Newmarket, and the leading citizens of that town and its vicinity. They were not party men, not political friends of Sir William Mulock coming here to boost his election, but men who came in their capacity as citizens, laying aside all party differences, and asking us, in the interest of the town of Newmarket and the riding of North York, to undertake this work. I remember that delegation very well; it was one of nearly one hundred, certainly more than fifty. So large was it, at all events, that there was not room in the ordinary rooms of ministers to receive it. We had to get the use of the Railway Committee room for the purpose, and there man after man rose up and told us that this was not a party question, but that they asked us, in the name of the town of Newmarket and the riding of North York, to give them that improvement.
Now, is the Holland river to be improved? If a boat is to be taken from Lake Simcoe to Newmarket it cannot be taken any other way than the way contemplated by the present work. My hon. friend tells us now that all these representations made to us by men of his own political persuasion were ridiculous, and if I am now to take the word of Conservatives in the House of Commons, the Conservatives in the town of Newmarket land the riding of North York are not trustworthy and their representations are to be treated with contempt. This is the position after all. My hon. friend told us we had not taken any precaution to ascertain whether ot not there would be any business for that canal when built. That is not fair. We had the representations of these -men all. My hon. friend told us we had not treated their statements with the contempt with which my ihon. friends opposite now treat them. We treated them as the representations of honest men, but my hon. friends say no, this whole thing is ridiculous. We complied with the requests of these men, and are we to be told that we did a corrupt action because we took their statements and representations as those of honest men? Yet that is the



position hon. gentlemen opposite are taking in order to make a point against the government. These gentlemen are ready to throw -contempt on men of their own political persuasion in order to make a point against us. What was our answer to the petition presented by these -men? We did not tell them it was ridiculous. We told them it was worthy of consideration and that we would send an engineer to investigate. We did send- an engineer, and he reported that the work could be done for some $300,000. Well, we thought that if we could have that useful work done for the town of Newmarket and the riding of North York for an expenditure of $300,000 we ought to do it. It turns out, however, that the work is -costing more than was expected. That is not unusual in works of this character. My hon. friend says it is going to cost a million dollars. But even if it should, even if there be a mistake, that is verv different from a corrupt act. My hon. friend, however, will not make that distinction, and says it is a useless waste of money. That is not the impression I gathered from the debate. I was not present when my hon friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) spoke, but I remember a speech he made some two or three years ago on this same question. I admit that he then opposed the grant, but he also stated that there would be work for the canal, and the ground of his objection was that there would be no water for it. This is what he said on the I2th of July, 1905:
There is a very extensive manufacturing concern m Newmarket but there is no guarantee that that factory will remain -there a month. Any one conversant with business knows that if that factory at Newmarket had to be located again, it would not be located at Newmarket. It is not a town that is suitable for a factory such as this, and there is no guarantee that it will remain there.
That was all the exception he took, namely, that there was no guarantee that the factory would remain there. He did not say that there was no work for the canal, but he was not sure that the enterprise would remain where it was. But if the factory be -still there, I presume -there is -a fair amount of work to be -done.

I think I said a great deal more than that. Senator Campbell who then represented North York in this House, said the canal would be used to bring lumber up to th-at mill, and I said that the logs were hard wood and would not float. He, however, said they would float.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That was work to be taken to the town, but the products of the factory are to be taken out of the town, and all my hon. friend had to -say was that he was not sure the factory would Six WILFRID LAURIER;
be there for ever. But if he was sure it would be there for ever. I take it for granted he would be satisfied.
I can quite understand why the minister and his government have gone into this canal if he assumes that by my statement that is what I meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that is another evidence that we are not to trust Conservatives when they address us, whether as members of the House or as a delegation. If a delegation should ever again come to us as Conservatives and represent that what they want is not a party question and is for the advantage of the locality they represent, and if I should be still in the position I enjoy to-day, I shall profit by the lesson I have just learned and will tell them: You say now it is no party question, but you will make it one as soon as the work is done.
But before the vote was cast in this House, did the right hon. gentleman not hear from Conservatives that -this work was perfectly useless?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
Then why did you go on with it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was after we had listened to the Conservatives in North York and made up our minds and brought down the estimates.
Had there been any m-onejy spent on this work before that delegation of Conservatives and Reformers waited on the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is my hon. friend serious? I tell him very seriously there was none.
There was $25,000, as my right hon. friend will see if he will look up the record.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am satisfied there was no money spent until we heard of the project from that delegation.
$25,000 was spent on surveys in October, and the delegation waited on the right hon. gentleman in the February -following, after all this work had been done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There might have been a survey, but I do not understand that a survey is the work itself. What is the trend of this motion? It is that while this work i-s going on we should stop it. Why, even if a mistake has been made it would be a greater mistake not to go on. It is sometimes a mistake to do certain things, but once a thing has been undertaken it i-s best to follow it to the end. In this matter we have the Con-

servatives of the county of North York and of the House of Commons at variance, and I am disposed to listen to the voice of the Conservatives of North York.

The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has accused us on this side of the House of unworthily casting ridicule and contempt upon this work which had been advocated by a delegation, which, as, he says, was composed partly of Liberals and partly of Conservatives. He seems to be seized with amazement that any opposition to what we regard as an absurd expenditure should be offered by us in this House, considering that some Conservatives were members of that delegation. That certainly is a remarkable view to take of the duty of hon. gentlemen on either side of this House. The right hon. gentleman may establish that criterion, if he likes, for the members of his own party;-I do not now know how many of them will be prepared to accept it ; but if he supposes that hon. gentlemen on this side will refrain from criticising an unjust expenditure, simply because it is advocated by Conservatives as well as Liberals in the particular riding affected, I desire to tell him that he has absolutely mistaken the temper and disposition of hon. gentlemen on this side. He tells us that ridicule and contempt have been cast upon this undertaking by the lack of defence on the part of himself and his ministers. His concluding words declared that because $200,000 had been expended already on this manifestly absurd and useless undertaking, therefore we should go on and spend $800,000 or $900,000 more. To state the argument is to refute it. The severest condemnation of this undertaking is the reply of the three ministers who have spoken. The argument in defence of this proposal is two-fold. In the first place, the argument is that this work is feasible. Feasible ? Of course, it is feasible. If you spend $10,000,000, no doubt, you could build a canal in a portion of the country that now has no water communication at all-and the work might not be worth $10 when completed. If you spend enough money on this undertaking, I suppose you can construct the canal under discussion, unless the absolute lack of water stands in the way. Next the defence of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) is that Conservatives and Liberals have asked for this woTk. Well, perhaps you could embark upon many expenditures in different ridings in this country that would receive the support of some Conservatives and a great many Liberals. But does that absolve-the prime minister seems to think it does-the government as trustees for the people from all responsibility in connection with the expenditure of the public 100J
money? Does he lay down as a doctrine to be accepted by this House and by this country that, if you can get Conservatives and Liberals to demand a certain expenditure, and if you convince yourself that the undertaking can, be carried out within the revenues of the country, the government, without further consideration, should embark upon it ? I ask the Prime Minister, as I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals this afternoon, what estimate is he able to give to the members of this House as to the business to be done on that canal and the tonnage to be carried over it in one year? Is the Prime Minister prepared to offer an estimate?
As the right hon. gentleman remains silent, his silence when that question is put to him across the floor of this House is an absolute condemnation, not only of the enterprise itself, but of the conduct of his government in entering upon it. Have we so much money in this country that we are ready to put a million or a million and a half into any enterprise, provided that money will carry it out, and provided that some Liberals and some Conservatives go to the government and ask for it? Yet, I leave it to hon. members who have listened to the Prime Minister and to the gentlemen who preceded him, whether there has been any defence of this undertaking otheT than that I have just mentioned. The right hon. gentleman seems to hint that it is a reproach to us for attacking this unjustifiable expenditure that three or four or half a dozen Conservatives advocated it three or four years ago. He seems to forget that what that delegation asked for, as I have understood it, was not the construction of a canal at a cost of a million or a million and a quarter of dollars, but the dredging of the Holland river; and, as pointed out by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) I venture to think that the enterprise had been already engaging the attention of the government, because it appears they had spent some $25,000 in surveys before that delegation was brought down. It looks very much as if the delegation had been brought down for the purpose of the enterprise, and that it did not initiate the enterprise in the mind of the government.
That is perfectly correct, as I know.

Without knowing the facts, that is what I should be in dined to think the true explanation of this case. So far as this expenditure is concerned, there has been absolutely no defence worthy of the name made in this House to-day. There is no estimate-there never has been an estimate-of the traffic to be carried on the canal. When all parts of this country, as my hon. friend

from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, are clamouring for the expenditure of public money in aid of transportation, the government, in their flush times, when they used to ask from their supporters throughout the country applications for the expenditure of public money, handed out a million and a quarter of dollars with no more benefit to the people than if they had thrown it into the sea-with less benefit, indeed, because, as the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has said, not only will the money spent in the work be wasted, but if it is attempted to maintain the canal, from $20,000 to $40,000 a year must be taken from the public revenues for that purpose. I do not desire to prolong this discussion. There has been no defence of this expenditure from the mouth of any minister. The right hon. Prime Minister tells us that he has given us his mind in this case. Perhaps he has. But I venture to think that if that is all that has been in his mind about it, he quite justifies the boast he made during the late election campaign, that he could not be troubled with so small matters as questions of proper or improper expenditure of the public moneys, that his soul-as he quaintly expressed it- is turned to higher things. I do not know whether that is a very great advantage to the people of this country after all. It seems to me that if his soul, on this occasion, could have been turned to the question of the traffic that would probably go over that canal, if his soul could have been turned to a consideration of the business aspects of this enterprise, that would have inured more to the true interest of the people than some of these eloquent phrases which we hear from the right hon. gentleman both in this House and on the public platform. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the expenditure is absolutely undefended. If a judge in a court were addressing a jury on the arguments pro and con in connection with this expenditure, he would be obliged to tell the jury that it was an absolutely undefended case. That is the way it stands before parliament and before the people of this country to-day. No minister of the Crown has ventured to say that there was the slightest estimate or consideration of the traffic that would go through that canal. The Minister of Railways and Canals told me that very frankly across the floor of the House this afternoon. When I asked the Prime Minister, after he had spoken upon this question and endeavoured to justify this expenditure, if he could give me the slightest idea as to what traffic will go over those four and a half miles of canal, he sat silent in his seat and returned no answer whatever.	And yet the Prime Minister
tells us that it was not a purely political enterprise-	Under these circumstances I
venture to submit that the resolution which has been proposed in this House is a proper one, and that, to use the words of that reso-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
lution, this is an absolutely ' wanton misuse and waste of public money.'
