Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Trent canal construction, 81,000,000.
How much of this vote will be devoted to opening out the two ends of the canal into Lake Ontario and the Georgian Bay?

GRAHAM (Minister of Railways) As a matter of fact the contract for the western end into the Georgian bay has not been let at all and no money out of this vote will be spent on it. The outlet to the Bay of Quinte has been let to Larkin & Sangster.
Has the whole work of connecting the navigable waters of Rice Lake to the Bay of Quinte been placed under contract?
There are two contracts not yet let.

Is it not the intention of the minister to go on with the opening of the western end at once? It would seem to me to be the most important part of the work. Until the ends of the canal are opened up the canal will be useless for the purpose for which it was designed.
When does the minister expect to place under contract the section between Lake Simcoe and the Georgian bay?
We have had two surveys made and the report on one of them at least has not yet been placed before me in its entirety.
Were there not three surveys?

One by the Severn river and the other by Kempenfeldt bay. No decision will be arrived at until my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) will have full opportunity to come down with a deputation of his friends and advocate what he thinks is the better route.
If the deputation has both Liberals and Conservatives on it I suppose the thing wdll go?
As I said at Barrie during the last campaign, whichever the engineer thinks the more feasible route will be accepted.

When the minister referred to this matter in Barrie during the last campaign the people living along the valley of the Nottawasaga river inferred from his remarks that the canal would surely be built along the valley of that river. As a matter of fact the county of Simcoe has appointed a committee on canals to take the question up, and the chairman of that committee has written to me to know if I could ascertain whether there has been a survey and a report made. If the question is considered on its merits it will be found that the canal can be built much more cheaply via Kempenfeldt bay and the Nottawasaga river than by way of the Severn river, because there is nothing but sand and gravel and clay on the western route whilst on the eastern route there will be a tremendous amount of rock cutting, and as every engineer knows one yard of rock cutting will cost about twelve times as much as a yard of gravel. I strongly urge that the minister give favourable consideration to the western route. Notable engineers of the past who have surveyed these routes unhesitatingly give their opinion in favour of the Kempenfeldt bay or Barrie-Nottawasaga river route. I strongly urge the advisability of completing the report as soon as possible so that I may

have the opnortunity of bringing down here a lot of good Reformers to interview the minister, and incidentally I suppose I may be allowed to bring a few Conservatives who are also interested in the matter. There is no doubt but that the western route is the easiest and the best route. It was the route followed by the early voyageurs; it was the war route in 1812, and from an engineering standpoint in the present day it is undoubtedly the most acceptable. Then, I would urge upon the government that they should seriously consider the advisability of making it a modern canal from Lake Simcoe on and not have it in the same category as the canal on the Trent route. The cost of making the locks larger and the waterway deeper would be comparatively small once the plant is erected there, and what a magnificent idea it would be to have these large freighters coming into Lake Simcoe and discharging their cargoes at Beaverton or at this dock at Holland Landing. The minister will be well advised if he does not give the preference to the Severn river route, althouffh during the last campaign a supporter of the government was elected m that riding. This canal has been a political question for so many years that it is time for us to call quits and turn it into a business enterprise at last.
The Lake Simcoe Dredging Company had a contract dated April 7, 1906, which they were in default with respect to. Did they get back their deposit of $4,649?
No; we forfeited it.
Did they get the balance of $750 which they claimed?
Not yet.
Are they still claiming it?
They still claim and the matter is under consideration.
Did they get anything?
They got about $1,600 on progress estimates for work done.
Is that all they are going to get?
I think so; the $700 is under consideration.

On July 15,
1908, tenders were called for a second letting and the lowest was $94,960 and the highest $167,023. Why was not the contract let on these tenders?
The figure was so much larger than the original contract that
'Your Engineer's' estimate was $131,000.

I did not say the estimate; I say the figure was so much larger than for the other contract which had been cancelled that I did not consider the matter so urgent that I should not look into it thoroughly. I had not the engineer's estimate with me at the time as I was away from the department and I would not accept it without inquiry.
It never was accepted?
No. If the approaching elections had anything to do with it, I would have let the contract immediately to get men to work.
My information is from prominent men in Newmarket, that political friends of the hon. gentleman's party were interested in the contract, and that they dare not let it to the lowest tenderer.
Nonsense.

Will the hon. gentleman explain in what way Mr. Widdifield is identified with almost every lot that has been taken and paid for in damages
there?

Mr. Widdifield, a lawyer, is the agent of the Minister of Justice, and as such passes the titles when we take possession of the lands. We do this, not directly, but through the Department of Justice, which has an agent at each of these places.
Does the minister know whether or not Mr. Widdifield has any personal connection with or interest in these lands?
I do not know. The business is not done through my department.
The reason I ask is that there are some lots in which neither Widdifield nor the other agent appears, but the parties deal directly with the department.

I do not think there is
any case in which there is no agent. There must be a legal agent representing the Department of Justice.
There are two cases in which there is no agent. _
I am informed that they cannot be for that.
Is each of the parties who is indemnified for drowned land paid the full amount of the cheque issued to Widdifield?
I think there is no question about that.
There was a question about it many times. We have had many instances in which the farmer who was being indemnified had 20 per cent commission taken from the amount of the cheque for party purposes.
In any of these cases?
In none of these cases, but there was a ease only a few years ago.
What is the name of the other agent?
Williams. He is also an agent of the Department of Justice.

I may say, for the information of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) that in all cases in which damages were paid in the county of Peterborough, the full amount was paid to the people who had the damaged land. There was no deduction in any case.
Was the cheque a joint cheque?
Yes, but there was no such deduction made as the hon. member for Victoria alleges. The Department of Justice itself paid for the legal work done by the solicitor.

The instance to which I had reference was an old one. I referred to the drowned land around Cameron lake, in which the agent of the government, part of the time, took 20 per cent commission from the people. But we discussed that, and I presume the practice was stopped. I desire to ask the minister about the surveying of the drowned land. I happen to know that at the present time in the county of Peterborough an engineer is surveying the drowned land and that he does not start from any known level of the canal or waterway, but just goes by the water mark on the trees. I am not finding any fault with him, because he is one of the most honourable men in the country; but it strikes me that there should be some datum point from which to take the level.
The chief engineer informs me that that is done in every case.

Then, the man who is doing it does not seem to know that. Will the minister give us the data concerning the dam being erected at Lindsay? Is the water going to be higher than before, or lower? Is it going to be maintained at an even level, or is it going to be allowed to fall to five or six feet below the top of the dam? Are there fish slides in the dam and passages for small launches?

The intention is not to raise the water, but to keep it at a level. The question of fish slides is one on which
there is a difference of opinion. Within the past ten days I have discussed that question with a deputation that came to see me on other matters, and their opinion was that where there were locks a fish slide was not necessary or satisfactory. The fish pass through when the locks are opened, while the fish slides get clogged up in a few weeks. With regard to small launches, there is no provision beside the ordinary locks.
The minister promised that he would provide a small lock or something of that kind.
We have considered the question of putting in intermediary gates, but we have not decided on it yet.
What size of boat will the locks accommodate?
Six feet in depth and 122 feet in length. All the details are in the report.
How many acres of land have been taken for this Newmarket canal?
The amount paid so far is about $27,000. I cannot tell the number of acres. That is worked out elsewhere. The hon. gentleman will find it in the report page 97-134 x 33 x 5.
Have you settled all the land damages at Newmarket down to Cook's bay?
Nearly all settled. There may be two or three cases yet to be settled.

The lock-master at Fenelon Falls has for a number of years been in the habit of raising and lowering the waters. Sometimes there would be a difference of two feet between the extreme high and the extreme low water caused by the eccentricities of this young gentleman. Consequently for weeks at a time, the water will be up on the shore and when winds come along those who own lands on the shore occasionally see portions of them floating down the lake. In other words considerable damage is done along the shores of that lake owing to the high waters. Is the minister paying damages caused by that class of irregularity ? There are a number of gentlemen there who have claims of that nature. Has he paid similar damages elsewhere? I understand damages nave been paid at Stony lake and also Rice lake.
We have paid damages for raising the permanent level of the water on Stony and Rice lakes but not in any case such as my hon. friend mentions.
You should.
What amount is to be spent on the eastern end of the Trent Valley canal now under contract ?
There will not be more than $200,000 spent on the Holland river and the balance will be spent on the main canal.

I understood the minister to say that there were a couple of sections not under contract on the eastern portion of the canal. What amount will be required to build them, and how long will it take to provide an eastern outlet into Lake Ontario?
. Mr. GRAHAM. I .should imagine it would take four years. I could not tell what would be the cost oi those sections as they are not let.
When do you expect to let the contract for the Healy Falls section and the one outlet at Rainy Falls ?

It is difficult to say. I am not getting as large appropriations for the canal this year as I would like. I tried to have the amount doubled but was not able. The Healy Falls contract might possibly be let during the autumn, but no work will be done this yeaT and I would not like to make a promise that it will be let. I want to go on as rapidly as the finances of the country will permit.

The finances of the country are all right. What is wanted is more energy. This thing has been dawdling on since 1833, and it is just wasting money to have it go on as it is. I had hoped that the minister, having come here full of vigour and energy, would have set an example and if he had not been given his way in getting this work completed, he would have resigned and brought on a crisis in the cabinet.
That would not help it.
I am not so sure. We are told that the cabinet was brought to time by a minister threatening to resign and also by the Finance Minister in like manner.
My resignation would not have that effect.

- I would not take that line until all other means had been tried and failed. The minister should first try his persuasive power in order to get this thing completed. In its present condition it is an eyesore, having a long complete stretch in the centre but the two ends unfinished. I want to draw attention to two things-the lighting and the opening of the locks. The department has a very good system of lighting by acetylene gas buoys. Along this canal you could have a number Mr. HUGHES.
of piers constructed on which these automatic buoys would be placed, and in that way the waterways could be lighted. There is a great deal of travel on these waters at night, and it is an immense advantage to have them well lighted. A part of the line around Lindsay and Fenelon Falls could be lighted by electricity. But between Lindsay and Sturgeon lake and above Lindsay to Port Perry, which could not be lighted by electricity, these piers could be readily constructed. There is another point to which I wish to draw attention. The locks are very burdensome to operate. You use the old winch system which came down from the time of Moses. I would suggest to the minister that he should bring that part of his department up to the 20th century and get a proper system of opening the locks along the line. All it requires is a little energy. The minister has a deputy who is willing, and if he will set his energy at work, he will not allow this old fashioned system to continue.

I think the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) is quite right with regard to the improvements that might be made and on the modern locks that are being constructed. So far as I can observe, the department is dealing with that aspect of the case. I would like to point out that the lakes might be better buoyed and lighted. I was going to Lindsay one night last fall myself, and stayed out nearly all night, not being able to find the way. It would be much better for the passenger boats if the lake were buoved, and there is no doubt that the passage into Lindsay and up the Scugog is dangerous, and should be better lighted. And, now that there is sufficient power to light by electricity, I would be willing to support the hon. member for Victoria in advocating the proper lighting of these channels.

Has it been decided what kind of locks are to be put in at Healy Falls? It is a great pity that the minister has not included in the estimates this year enough to complete the lower end of this canal. It is a very important work. The minister, when asked when we might expect it to be finished, said in about four years. He knows that the Healy Falls portion is a very difficult one. I think that, even if he lets the contract next year, it will be many years before it can be finished. The same is true of the portion just below the village of Campbellford at Raney's Falls. Had the money devoted to the work that was so long under discussion this afternoon been expended on these portions of the canal, it would have been of much greater benefit to the country. I do not pretend to be very well posted on this subject beyond the information we have gathered in the discussion to-day, but considering the defence made by the ministers

one can hardly come to any other conclusion than that the money spent on the Neymarket canal will be practically thrown away. There has been a good deal of speculation as to just where this canal is going to run. I would like to ask the minister to tell us if he has yet decided whether it is to follow the river at Raney's Falls, and what kind of locks they intend to place at Healy Falls?

At Healy Falls, we will follow the river with the ordinary lift-lock. I think my hon. friend will see that it would not be wise, in the public interest, to announce what we are going to do at Campbellford at this time.
Some Campbellford people tell us the canal is going to follow the bed of the river, while others say it will go along the bank.

They will not follow the bed of the river at Campbellford. I desire to draw the attention of the minister to two branch canals, of one of which, the Haliburton branch, I have already spoken. The minister has never been up that route. In order to impress the officers of the department with the importance of keeping the water up to a certain level, I got two of the officers in a boat out in a lake and succeeded in running themj aground. Fortunately, or unfortunately, a very violent storm arose. There was no chaplain aboard, so I had to officiate in receiving their final confession, because they thought they were going to kingdom come. If we could get the minister or deputy minister to come up there, I promise I will look after their safety. But I would like the privilege of showing them that the Haliburton canal is an absolute necessity and that it mav be easily constructed. The waterway is there and the construction of six locks would open up sixty miles of navigation. It would assist in developing a very fine country and bringing out valuable hardwood timber, such as maple and birch now so largely used in the manufacture of furniture, and bringing it out in the only way possible, because no railway will be put in there. But I have already spoken on this subject, and will not detain the committee now. Another point to which my attention was drawn bv the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) was this: Muskoko lake and Lake Couchiching are on nearly the same level, and a little work would open u.t>
the connecting link between these waters, that is between the waters of Severn river and Muskoka lake, and so bring Bracebridge, Gravenhurst and a large area of country into water communication with the outer world, that is, if this canal is ever to be completed. Now, I would like to ask if the minister has looked into the Haliburton canal? I may say that we have ways and means of directing the attention .of the government to these things. This is a new parliament, and I am giving the hon. gentleman a preliminary canter on this subject this session. But I promise him that next session, if something is not done meantime, we will make it considerably more interesting, and will continue in that way until we impress upon the minister, even better than a deputation of Grits and Tories could do it. that something ought to be done in this matter.

I have not paid much attention to these branch lines that have been mentioned several times. To be frank with the committee, I do not feel inclined to undertake more branch lines than the present, nor until we get the main line through. When that is done, I think it will be reasonable to discuss some betterments to connect with other places.

Is it the intention of the department to dredge between Trent bridge and Hastings, or between Hastings and Rice lake this summer? I had the privilege of taking a little trip there last summer, and like my hon. friend from Victoria, we did not know whether we were going to get back the same night or not ran on the rocks. That part of the river is used to a considerable extent during the summer, and it would not be a very difficult or expensive proposition to have the work done.
I think it is under contract.

I am very glad to hear that.
Patent Record-further amount required, $9,000.

Is there really any good purpose served by printing that large pamphlet called the 'Patent Record'? I think all the members receive it, and I was wondering whether there was any necessity for getting so many of them printed. Possibly it could be done away with.

The expenditure is largely due to the cuts of the different patents. It is a book that inventors are anxious to have, as without it they would have no record of inventions, and they might he working on an invention which had been already recorded. It is sent to all the public libraries in the country. The total cost is $17,000 or $18,000 a year. This year we have to pay up a lot of arrears. It costs $1,800 or $1,900 a month. At the beginning of this year we were in arrears some nine months, now we are in arrears only three months.
Year-book-further amount required, $4,600-

How many Yearbooks are printed and distributed every

year, and how many are the members allowed to have for the purpose of distribution?
There are 11,000 printed each year, 7,000 in English and 4,000 in French. I am told that 5 or 6 are sent to each member.
What proportion of them are bound in cloth and what proportion in paper? WThen bound in cloth they make a very nice book for a library.

I am told there are about
4,000	bound in cloth, and these are chiefly sent out to libraries and places where we know they will be preserved. Those bound m paper are sent out for ordinary distribution.
Further amount required for the development of the dairy and fruit industries, and the improvement and transportation of, and the promotion of the sale and trade in food end other agricultural products, $13,000.
What is the whole amount of which this is supplementary?
The whole amount last year was $125,000. The reason for this vote is almost entirely due to some arrears of accounts with the railroads for the refrigerator cars.	~
Will the amount be less another year?

We will ask for the same amount as we ask for this year, without these arrears.
Mr- Ih A. GORDON. I would like to ask the minister if he has considered the advisability of including in some such estimate as this, a sum sufficient to erect a cold storage warehouse to experiment in the handling of apples. I may point out that Kent county has the greatest number of apple trees I believe of any county in the Dominion, but, our orchards are going to waste seemingly because the farmers are not in a position to handle their crops to advantage. I believe it is largely owing to the fact that the cold storage warehouses are not in the vicinity of the orchards, and there has not been sufficient development along that line to induce people to invest m building them. I think an experimental warehouse for that purpose is absolutely essential, and 1 hope the minister will promise that a sufficient sum will be included to make a testing station, and let us see if we cannot handle the apple crop to better advantage. To-day, although there are so many apple trees in that vicinity, you cannot get an apple at any price, whereas in the city of Ottawa apples at $8 to $9 per barrel are coming in from the eastern end of the country where they are properly handled >
presume largely owing to assist-Mr. U. WILSON.
ance offered by the Dominion and local governments.

The proposition the hon. gentleman makes would more naturally come under the vote foT cold storage warehouses. That vote is under a statute, and the statute does not provide for such an experiment as the hon. gentleman talks of. I have no doubt myself that one of the most important necessities for our apple trade is a means for cooling apples immediately, or very soon after, they are picked, and before they are shipped. The fruit, if copied down as low as possible without being frozen, will keep much better afterwards than in ordinary storage, or in ordinary cars for shipment. No doubt one of the main improvements which the apple trade must look to is cold storage facilities close to the orchards, where the fruit can be cooled as soon as possible after it is picked. I have not in my vote for the coming fiscal year any provision for such an experiment as my hon. friend has outlined. I had hoped that the provision for cold storage warehouses under the Act would be sufficient to meet the necessities which my hon. friend has alluded to. It is possible that the circumstances and conditions in the fruit districts are not such that the people are able to fully take advantage of the provisions of the cold storage Act and if so perhaps it would be well to amend that Act or to provide other facilities which would meet the necessities of the case. But in the estimates for the coming fiscal year I must say there is no provision for such an experiment as my hon. friend outlined.

I believe the sum required will not exceed $12,000 or $15,000 for one station of that character. I would not hesitate, realizing the importance of this work, to recommend in the strongest language possible that a movement be made to introduce an amendment at once for the purpose of this experiment. As I understand we have to be educated as to the methods that we must adopt in order to take care of the crop in a proper way, and the only way that we can ascertain the best method is by having an experimental warehouse. Personally I feel like adopting a much more comprehensive method but it may be well to go slowly under the circumstances and take up the matter in this way as suggested. 1 hope the minister will not allow the opportunity to go by, because I am satisfied our farmers are not getting 25 per cent of what they should for their apples. Last fall I know apples were marketed at prices ranging from 8 to 25 cents per hundred simply because there was no provision whereby they could care for the ai>ples and market them as the country would be prepared to absorb them and pay the price. I believe the House is convinced

that if the apples can be kept in proper condition and be delivered in the fall, winter and spring in good condition that people will not only demand them but pay the price. Matters of this kind are so important that we should not neglect the opportunity to assist this industry. In one night we passed military estimates aggregating $6,000,000 and if we are satisfied that cold storage is the proper means for the handling of the apple crop, so that the greatest advantage shall accrue to the farmers, we should not hesitate to undertake the expenditure of a small sum for that purpose. 1 trust that the resources of the minister will not only provide the funds but will also indicate the best way in which to put this system into operation.

A farmer in my county who has a large apple orchard has built a cold storage warehouse at his own expense to handle his own apples and those of his neighbours. If the suggestion of the hon. member is carried out, will that man receive fair treatment and have a fair proportion of the expenses to which he has been put refunded to him ? If he does not receive a refund, I think all should be treated alike. If one part of the country builds its own cold storage warehouses I do not see why we should help others. I have sometimes thought that these are things that should be left very largely to the people themselves. A great deal has been done in this work and I feel that anything that can be done to help our farmers-I do not mean the agriculturists, the men who work the farmers-will be liberally supported by this House.

I am very glad to hear the remarks of my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. D. A. Gordon). I consider this one of the most important questions that we could consider in this House. There is no question that the apple crop this year was good in most parts of the country, but owing to want of cold storage, the farmers have not received the remuneration they should have received. The result is that many orchards throughout Ontario are not cared for as they would be if it was a paying business. The agriculturists and fruit growers do not receive the consideration in matters of this kind to which they are entitled. We spend millions on the militia, we pass these items without consideration, whereas it is exceedingly difficult to obtain any substantial assistance for the farming community. I hope that the remarks which have been made will receive consideration and that next year the estimates will contain a substantial amount for the encouragement of farmers to build these cold storage warehouses. We may have enterprising men such as the gentleman mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. U. Wilson) who will build such warehouses, but they are few, and I
do not think the farmers are called upon to pay for cold storage warehouses. I think they should have assistance from the government.

I am pleased to learn that Lennox county contains men who have gone so extensively into the fruit growing that they are able to build cold storage warehouses for themselves. I agree with the hon. member for Kent (Mr. D. A. Gordon) that this is a very important question and that the very small amount spent in the interests of the farmers in the past might be doubled or trebled and still the farmers would not be getting anything like their fair share of public expenditure. If we had as the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Gordon) suggested, even one proper cold storage warehouse at some point where it could be utilized and where the farmers would be able to experiment with it, we would be in a position to know the full value of such assistance. Hundreds and thousands of dollars worth of fruit go to waste every year. At present we have a system of co-operation in many parts of the province where the farmers ship their own apples. Where that system is in vogue, if we had what the hon. member for Kent (Mr. D. A. Gordon) suggests, a cold storage plant to which the farmers could ship apples and keep them properly until the market developed, it would be a great advantage to the farmer and I think the minister might well consider this question. What amount did the government pay last year for refrigerator car service ?
I have here accounts for 1908 amounting to over $9,600, and we paid something during the summer. I would think the total amount would be from $13,000 to $14,000, speaking from memory.
That is not a very great donation.
That has served the purpose.

In Wentworth a co-operation plan has been organized and the details pretty well arranged to construct a cold storage warehouse for apples in particular, and while under the general Gold Storage Act this establishment would come in for some encouragement it seems to be the pretty general opinion that perhaps that encouragment could be increased in an experimental way and as no vote could do more in the general interest of the country than something to encourage an improvement along agricultural lines, the consensus of opinion seems to be that if this vote could be increased, it would be generally approved and result in great good not only in the counties of Wentworth

and Kent but in other places, particularly in two or three of the large fruit and apple growing centres.
It is a question of so much importance that the House should impress on the Minister of Agriculture to increase the grant in this respect,

It is impossible to overstate the influence that the Department of Agriculture under the present minister has had on the creation of wealth in this country. Any real addition to our national wealth must come from our natural resources, and I know from personal contact wth farmers that they appreciate very highly the Minister of Agriculture as their representative in this government. I am fully in accord with every proposition that has proceeded from the government so far in relation to the important matter of affording cold storage for the perishable products of the farm, and I should be glad if we may witness a large extension of that part of the work of the Department of Agriculture. The suggestion from the hon. member from Kent (Mr. Gordon) is well worthy the attention 'of the minister, and I sincerely hope that the gentlemen who have spoken on this question will have the satisfaction of learning that there will be a larger measure of cold storage in future than we have known of in past experience. In the one item of apples alone I find that in my own county there are more bushels of apples produced annually than the total quantity of barrels exported from this country, which would seem to indicate that large quantities of apples go to waste for want of proper attention. I trust that the Minister of Agriculture will see his way clear to devise some method by which in a good many localities in the province of Ontario, in the fruit season, the people may be able to avail themselves more fully of the advantages of cold storage.

The Act under which bonuses are given to cold storage warehouses covers such as would be required for the apple trade. I know that some people have felt that another arrangement of the bonus than that provided in the Act would be more likely to encourage the building of ccld storages for this particular trade. I confess that I have been considering somewhat whether the terms of the bonus may be modified to meet the particular necessities of this kind of cold storage. I shall be very glad to arive at a favourable conclusion because I am very anxious that ample cold storage facilities should be provided. The trouble with cold storage for apples alone is that while a building is very necessary during the short season of the apple crop, apples are bulky and take up much space, and the profit on the venture has to be made in a very short period of the year. That makes it a difficult prob-Mr. SEALEY.
!em. I shall be glad to further consider the question of changing in some degree the conditions of the cold storage bonus for such a cold storage warehouse, for I have closely at heart the providing of warehouses for the apple trade. The organization of the fruit growers' asociations was initiated by the officers of my department and I believe that sort of co-operation is one of the best means of handling our apple crop. These associations have done excellent work and have set a good model for the country at large.
Further amount required to pay for the construction of branch of the electric railway to the Central Experimental Farm, including cost of fence, $10,500.
Is this road on the farm or to the farm?
The road is double-tracked, about a mile long within the farm and it is only the part within the farm that we had anything to do with.
What is it used for?

Thousands and thousands of visitors come to the experimental farm every year, and before this arangement was made they had to drive in cabs, or walk about a mile and a half. As a Tesult of insistent demands from the public I made an arrangement with the electric railway company that if they would build to the boundary of the farm we would build the road within the farm.
What is the total cost?
$39,889. The estimate of cost was made and approved of by the chief engineer of the Railway Department who drew the plans. The electric railway company constructed it on that estimate.

It seems to me that this is a very large amount for constructing a mile of railway and if there be such a large number of visitors to the farm the road ought to pay for itself. Should not the electric company have built this road themselves in view of the profits they would receive from it, or at least should they not have paid half the cost? Do they give a service in winter?
Yes.
Do they give a five cent fare to the general public and the servants of the farm?

Yes, and they also carry the mails free to and from the farm. This has been under discussion for years; the service was very strongly demanded by the visitors to the farm and it was only when we agreed to this that the . railway would build to the farm, boundary. I venture to think that during the coming summer it

will repay for all the outlay and a good deal more.
Who did the work?
It was done by the Ottawa Electric Railway Company on the estimates and under the supervision of our own Railway Department.
Does the government own the road?
Yes.
What proportion of this item will be expended on the fencing?

About $600. We have to fence both sides of the track, because it runs through the field where the cattle are and through the orchard. The only part of the road we are paying for is that which runs through the farm.
Does this complete the payment?

Yes.
Quarantine - further amount required. $14,000.
What was the total amount expended this year?

The amount voted in the main estimates was $100,000 and we ask for this in addition. In the year before about $125,000 was spent.
